names.name: Alabama white sauce wings
names.said: In north Alabama, white sauce needs no adjective. Everywhere else it needs the state's name in front of it.

text.what: Wings smoked over hickory and then coated or dunked in white sauce — a mayonnaise-based barbecue sauce with vinegar, lemon juice, black pepper, salt, and in many versions cayenne and horseradish. It is thin, sharp and pale, and it goes on at the end of the cook rather than during it, because mayonnaise breaks over heat. The result is tangy rather than sweet, with none of the tomato or molasses a reader expects from the word barbecue.
text.story:
Bob Gibson invented it in Decatur, Alabama in 1925, at Big Bob Gibson Bar-B-Q, and it was used on chicken. That is the fact every account agrees on: the sauce, the man, the town, the year, the bird.

The method is recorded as smoke first, then dunk. Alabama's barbecue is a chicken-and-hickory tradition as much as a pork one, and white sauce is the sauce that goes with the chicken.

It stayed a north Alabama thing for most of a century. The sauce was bottled and sold commercially from 1994, which is when it began appearing outside the region.

*Tradition holds —* the mayonnaise is there to keep white meat from drying over a long smoke, the fat standing in for basting. This project could not source that explanation to a document and marks it as the story the tradition tells rather than an established reason.

*Inference —* the wing is a later and smaller application of a whole-chicken sauce. Nothing in the sources searched here dates a first white-sauce wing or names the cook who made one.
text.how: Rub the wings with salt and pepper and smoke them over hickory until the skin renders and the meat is done through — some pits finish them hot, over direct heat or in oil, because a slow smoke leaves wing skin slack. Then dunk: a pan of white sauce, the wings in and straight out, so the coat is thin and even. Sauce at the end and off the heat, because mayonnaise splits. Serve with more of the same in a cup. The sauce keeps in the fridge and sharpens for a day or two.
text.today: Bottled white sauce sells nationally and turns up on wing boards a long way from Decatur, where it usually arrives as a dip rather than a coat. *Inference —* it reads to most American drinkers as a rival to ranch, which is not what it is: white sauce is a vinegar sauce built on mayonnaise and meant to go on hot meat, and ranch is a cold buttermilk-and-herb dressing meant for dipping.

kin.as: The sauce itself — mayonnaise, vinegar, lemon, pepper — invented in Decatur in 1925 and bottled from 1994.
Where the sauce was made and where the smoke-then-dunk method is recorded.

names.name: Lemon pepper wings
names.said: The order is a count, a cut and a state: twenty, all flats, lemon pepper wet.

text.what: A wing cooked without breading and finished in lemon pepper — granulated lemon zest mashed with cracked black pepper, then baked and dried, usually with salt and sugar in the blend. Atlanta orders it two ways. Dry means the seasoning goes on alone. Wet means a sauce underneath it, butter or a lemon sauce or Buffalo, with the dry seasoning shaken over the top. The wing plate comes with fried rice at a great many Atlanta counters, and Wikipedia calls the dish emblematic of the city's cuisine.
text.story:
Lemon pepper is a commercial product before it is a wing. William Shoffeitt, a product engineer in Healdsburg, California, launched the blend in July 1967 through Shoffeitt's Enhance Seasoners, sold it along the West Coast, and moved it through trade shows and department stores including Sears and JCPenney. It was aimed at seafood.

Atlanta turned it into a wing. Wikipedia's account is that people there began adding lemon pepper to Buffalo wings to cut the heat, and that the dish took hold in the mid-2000s — attributed in part to its not marking a white t-shirt the way an orange sauce does, which mattered to rappers wearing them. The wings are a fixture of Atlanta's strip clubs; Chris Kirschner of The Athletic reported that the food at those clubs, wings above all, drew celebrity customers. Keisha Lance Bottoms, before she was mayor, said in 2017: "Lemon pepper wings are Atlanta." Eric Kim wrote in The New York Times in 2022 that "in Atlanta, lemon pepper is queen," calling the wings "central to [the city's] social fabric."

The wet version's paper trail is knottier than the phrase suggests. Wikipedia credits its invention to the American Deli in Atlanta. The second episode of Atlanta put "lemon pepper wet" in a character's hands from J.R. Crickets — a restaurant that did not then have it on the menu, though it sold a similar item called Fester wings that customers already called lemon pepper wet; the show's writer Stephen Glover said he wanted the character hooked up with something off-menu, and the dish on screen was modelled on the American Deli's. J.R. Crickets added lemon pepper wet to the menu in 2017 in the show's honour. Mike Jordan of Eater Atlanta credited the episode with popularising it. So the restaurant most famous for the dish is not the restaurant credited with inventing it, and the fame arrived through television.

The wings run through Atlanta music and back out. 2 Chainz's "Hot Wings" (2018): "She just want her 20-piece/ All flats with the lemon pepper." Drake's "Lemon Pepper Freestyle" (2021) features Rick Ross, who owns Wingstop locations and has named them in several songs. In 2020 Lou Williams of the Los Angeles Clippers was nicknamed Lemon Pepper Lou after reports he ordered the wings with Jack Harlow at Magic City during a trip outside the NBA bubble; the club already sold a "Louwill Lemon Pepper BBQ Wings". He objected to the nickname, then trademarked it.
text.how: Fry the wing bare and hot. Dry: shake it in lemon pepper straight out of the oil while the skin still holds seasoning. Wet: toss it first in melted butter, a lemon sauce or Buffalo sauce, then hit it with the dry blend on top, so it reads sharp and salty over something slick. Wikipedia's own description says the wings are roasted rather than fried; Atlanta counters fry them, and *Inference —* the encyclopedia is describing a home method rather than the takeout window. Many shops use a premade blend rather than mashing zest into pepper themselves.
text.today: Chains sell lemon pepper nationally, and the flavour has spun off tacos, loaded fries, pierogies, pizza, beer and soda. It was already Wingstop's second-most-ordered Super Bowl flavour in the National Chicken Council's wing round-up, behind Original Hot and ahead of Hickory Smoked BBQ. *Inference —* Atlanta's version survives the export because what makes it local is the order rather than the recipe: the count, the all-flats, the wet-or-dry, and the fried rice under the plate.

names.name: Old Bay wings
names.said: Say Old Bay in Maryland and nobody asks which brand. The yellow can is the noun.

text.what: A wing finished in Old Bay — a blend of eighteen herbs and spices built in Baltimore in 1939, celery salt first, with red and black pepper and paprika, and bay leaves, mustard, cardamom, cloves and ginger among the rest. It goes on dry out of the fryer, or in butter as a wet toss, and it is the same can that goes on steamed blue crab, on fries, on popcorn and around the rim of a beer glass. Salt and celery seed do the work, not heat; a customer who wants heat adds hot sauce on top.
text.story:
The seasoning has a documented history and the wing does not.

Gustav Brunn built a wholesale spice business in Wertheim, Germany, moved it to Frankfurt, and was arrested after Kristallnacht and sent to Buchenwald. His wife paid a lawyer a large sum for his release; the family already held American visas and escaped to New York and then Baltimore, where Brunn had relatives. He arrived with a small spice grinder, founded the Baltimore Spice Company in 1939, and made "Delicious Brand Shrimp and Crab Seasoning", later renamed Old Bay after the Baltimore Steam Packet Company — the Old Bay Line — which ran passenger ships from Baltimore to Norfolk in the early 1900s. McCormick & Company of Hunt Valley bought the brand in 1990.

*Tradition holds —* the wing came later and came sideways, the way everything else in the Chesapeake got seasoned: the can was already on the counter. Wikipedia lists chicken wings among the things Old Bay is put on, alongside fried chicken, french fries, tater tots, corn, boiled peanuts, potato salad and guacamole, and notes that several movie theatres in the region keep it in the condiment section. This project found no source naming a first restaurant, a cook or a year for the wing itself, and none is asserted here.

The can's reach is easier to date than the wing's. Utz of Hanover, Pennsylvania built its Crab Chip on a similar blend; Herr's uses Old Bay itself; Lay's introduced Chesapeake Bay Crab Spice chips in 2018. Flying Dog brewed an Old Bay summer ale, Dead Rise, for the seasoning's 75th anniversary in 2014. McCormick released Old Bay Hot Sauce ahead of Super Bowl LIV in 2020; it sold out within thirty minutes, crashed the website, and $3.49 bottles resold online for between $50 and $200. Old Bay Goldfish crackers followed in 2022 and sold out online in nine hours. The can went from metal to plastic in 2017, and in December 2025 McCormick announced a return to metal.
text.how: Fry the wing bare so the skin is dry enough to hold powder, then shake it in Old Bay while it is still hot. Wet version: toss in melted butter first, then the seasoning, which gives a paste rather than a dust. Some kitchens mix Old Bay into the dredge as well as onto the finished wing; some steam or bake instead of frying, because the seasoning does not need a crust to read. Serve with whatever the bar pours — this is a seasoning, not a sauce, so blue cheese, ranch and vinegar all sit comfortably beside it.
text.today: Old Bay wings run on Maryland and Virginia bar menus, through the wider Mid-Atlantic, and into New England and the Gulf Coast where the can already travelled. McCormick sells an Old Bay hot sauce and several blend variants — with garlic, with lemon, with brown sugar — that put the same flavour on a wing by a different route. *Inference —* the style spreads with the can rather than with a recipe, which is why it has no founding restaurant to point at.

kin.as: The blend the whole style is — celery salt, red and black pepper, paprika and fifteen more, built in Baltimore in 1939.
The other American wing finished dry, though that rub comes off a smoker and this one comes off a crab pot.
Another city's seasoning wing, with citrus where this has celery seed.
The pair of words that decide whether the seasoning goes on bare or through butter.
What the wing has to be for a dry seasoning to stick — no batter to hide under.
Take the same can, at the same bar, in the same basket.
Built a business on a seasoned fry in the next state up, on the same Mid-Atlantic taste for spiced potatoes.
The style that made a wing a sauced thing; Old Bay answers with a wing that is seasoned and not sauced at all.
The yellow can is doing the same work a hot sauce label does — a regional identity you can hold.

confusable_with.tell: Look for celery salt and paprika without smoke. Old Bay is salty and celery-forward off a fryer; a Memphis rub carries smoke and comes off a pit.
Citrus. Lemon pepper leads with zest; Old Bay leads with celery seed and salt, and there is no lemon in the can.

names.name: Buffalo wings
names.said: In Buffalo nobody says 'Buffalo wings'. They say wings, and a medium order comes with blue cheese and celery whether you asked or not.

text.what: A chicken wing cut into a drumette and a flat, deep-fried bare — no batter, no flour — then shaken in a bowl with melted butter and a vinegar-based cayenne pepper sauce, and served hot with celery, carrot sticks and a dip of blue cheese or ranch. Heat runs mild, medium and hot, and the order names the heat before it names the count. The wing is named for Buffalo, New York, and has nothing to do with the animal.
text.story:
Chicken wings were cheap in 1964 because almost nobody ate them; they went into stock, into soup, or into the bin. Three stories explain what changed, and the Bellissimo family told all three.

In the first, Dominic Bellissimo was tending bar at the Anchor Bar on Main Street on a Friday night in March 1964 when friends turned up late, and his mother Teressa fried what she had and tossed it in cayenne sauce. In the second, which Dominic gave Calvin Trillin for The New Yorker in 1980, the midnight hour mattered: the bar's mostly Catholic drinkers could eat meat again at twelve, and he wanted something to hand them. In the third, Frank Bellissimo said a delivery went wrong — wings arrived instead of the backs and necks that went into the spaghetti sauce — and he asked Teressa to do something with them. Teressa sent the wings out with celery and blue cheese from the antipasto tray, and charged nothing for them.

John Young tells it differently, and told it first. Young moved to Buffalo from Stockton, Alabama in 1948, aged thirteen, and from 1961 sold whole uncut wings, breaded, deep-fried and drowned in a tomato-based sauce he called mumbo, at John Young's Wings 'n Things. A travelling boxer had told him about a restaurant in Washington, D.C. doing good business in wings, and he decided to specialise. Young registered the name at the county courthouse and left the area in 1970. He said the Anchor Bar did not carry wings as a regular menu item until 1974. A local newspaper profile of the Anchor Bar in 1969 does not mention wings; Duff's, across town, started selling them that same year. In 2013 the National Buffalo Wing Festival put John Young in its Hall of Flame.

The city settled nothing and celebrated anyway: in 1977 Buffalo issued a proclamation honouring Frank Bellissimo and named 29 July Chicken Wing Day. Trillin's 1980 piece carried the story out of western New York. Buffalo Wild Wings opened in 1982, Hooters in 1983, and the wing stopped being a Buffalo thing.
text.how: Cut the wing at both joints. Keep the drumette and the flat; the tip goes to stock. Fry bare at a high heat until the skin browns and crackles — no dredge, no batter, which is the line Buffalo draws against Rochester. Melt butter into cayenne pepper sauce, classically Frank's RedHot, sometimes Crystal, and hold it warm; more butter reads mild, less reads hot. Drop the wings into a metal bowl, pour the sauce over, and shake. Sauce goes on after the fryer, never before. Celery and carrots on the plate, blue cheese in a cup.
text.today: Every bar in America sells a version, and most sell it beside a dozen other flavours. Buffalo's own joints hold the line on bare frying, blue cheese and a plain orange sauce, and Visit Buffalo Niagara runs an official Buffalo Wing Trail of shops in the region. *Inference —* the style's name now travels further than its method: 'Buffalo' on a national menu marks the sauce, not the fry.

kin.as: Claims the invention, dates it to 4 March 1964, and has trademarked the phrase.
Sold breaded whole wings in mumbo sauce here from 1961, three years before the Anchor Bar's date.
Fried the wings the Anchor Bar's version turns on.
Cayenne pepper sauce cut with melted butter, and the whole of what makes a wing Buffalo.
Came off the bar's antipasto tray on the first night and never left the plate.
The dip Buffalo serves; asking for ranch marks you as from somewhere else.

Seventy miles east, breading the same bird — the nearest rival and the oldest argument.
Three Bellissimo stories, one John Young, and no document that settles it.

names.name: Jerk wings
names.said: Jerk names the rub, the marinade, the mop and the fire. One word does four jobs.

text.what: Wings dry-rubbed or wet-marinated in Jamaican jerk seasoning and cooked over fire until the outside blackens. Allspice and Scotch bonnet peppers carry it; cloves, cinnamon, scallions, nutmeg, thyme, garlic, brown sugar, ginger, soy sauce, vinegar and salt fill it out. The seasoning goes on before the heat, which is the whole difference from a wing that gets sauced after the fryer. Smoke comes from the fuel — pimento wood traditionally, charcoal in a split oil drum in most places that sell it — and the finish is char, not gloss. A scotch-bonnet sauce goes on afterward at the counter's discretion.
text.story:
Jerking is Taíno and Arawak before it is anything else. The Spanish historian Gonzalo Fernández de Oviedo y Valdés documented in 1516 how they cooked and preserved meat and fish on a barbacoa with native hot peppers — Scotch bonnet and cayenne — and pimento, sometimes wrapping meat in papaya leaves to tenderise it. The Spanish introduced pigs, cattle and chickens in the 1500s and adopted the method. When the English invaded Jamaica in 1655, the Spanish freed the people they had enslaved, who fled inland and became some of the first Jamaican Maroons; they intermarried with the remaining Taíno and took on the practice. By the end of the eighteenth century most groups had moved to imported pork, while the Maroons kept hunting wild hogs and jerking them.

The word travelled from charqui, a Spanish term of Quechua origin for dried meat, which also gives English jerky.

The equipment changed around the 1960s, when Caribbean entrepreneurs began cutting oil barrels lengthwise, drilling vents and hinging the lids to hold smoke — the barrel is now standard across the island and everywhere the trade went. Jerk followed the Caribbean diaspora into Britain, Canada and the United States, and the jerk stand or jerk centre turned up wherever the migration settled.

Brooklyn is one of those places. Gavin Hussey, called Peppa since his teens and born in St. Andrew Parish, Jamaica, co-founded Danny & Pepper's on Flatbush Avenue in 1995 and opened Peppa's Jerk Chicken on Flatbush about a decade later. Black-Owned Brooklyn's profile describes the birds washed in vinegar and charred until the skin crackles and blackens, with the house scotch-bonnet sauce added for more heat, and escovitch fish and festival on the same menu. The article does not mention wings.

*Inference —* jerk wings are a bar and takeout cut of a whole-bird method, and the record on jerk is written about chicken and pork rather than about wings. Nothing here dates a first jerk wing.

Jamaica trademarked Jamaica Jerk as a geographical indication in September 2015, the first English-speaking Caribbean country to register one, aimed at products sold as jerk abroad.
text.how: Make the seasoning: allspice and Scotch bonnet as the base, then whichever of cloves, cinnamon, nutmeg, thyme, scallion, garlic, ginger, brown sugar, soy and vinegar the house uses. Rub dry or marinate wet, and leave it on the meat for hours rather than minutes — the seasoning is a cure, not a coat. Cook over charcoal in a split drum with the lid down, or over pimento wood where it is available, turning until the outside goes black and the fat has rendered. Mop with the marinade as it cooks. Serve with hard dough bread, festival, bammy or fried dumplings, and hit it with pepper sauce at the table.
text.today: Jerk stands run in Brooklyn, the Bronx, Miami and Hartford, and jerk turns up on American chain wing boards as one flavour among a dozen: Jeremiah's Tavern in Rochester, read on 16 September 2026, listed Jamaican Jerk between Cajun Dry Rub and Iron Smoke. *Inference —* what survives the move onto a national board is the spice mix; the barrel, the wood and the hours of marinade do not, and the two things end up sharing a name.

names.name: Chicago mild sauce wings
names.said: The order is the cook and the sauce in four words: wings, fried hard, mild.

text.what: Wings fried hard — left in the oil past golden until the skin goes dark and brittle — then handed over a counter in a box with french fries and a slice of white bread, the whole box doused in mild sauce. Mild sauce is a tomato condiment of Chicago's Black South and West Sides: ketchup and tomato paste with sugar, vinegar and spices, pungent and sweet with a vinegar sting. It is a pour, not a toss. The sauce goes over everything in the box, and the bread and the fries take as much of it as the wings do.
text.story:
The sauce's history is recorded through the restaurants that poured it rather than through any single invention. America's Test Kitchen, writing on mild sauce in 2021, says flatly that "the origins of both sauces are murky" — meaning mild sauce and its Washington cousin, mumbo. Wikipedia names Harold's Chicken Shack, Uncle Remus Saucy Fried Chicken and Lem's Bar-B-Q as the restaurants that made it popular, and ties it to Black communities in Chicago.

The dates that do exist belong to the shops. Harold Pierce, who moved to Chicago in 1943 and worked as a chauffeur, opened Harold's Chicken Shack on 22 June 1950 at 47th and Kenwood; he and his wife Hilda also ran a soul food restaurant on 39th called the H&H, whose specialties were dumplings and chicken feet. Pierce let each franchisee build its own character rather than matching a template, so the constants across the chain are the chicken dinners and the emblem of a cook chasing a chicken with a cleaver, sometimes in lights, sometimes hand-painted, often with the cook dressed as a king. Redlining kept his expansion inside Black neighbourhoods, which is part of why the shacks concentrate on the South Side.

Argia B. Collins trademarked his own Chicago barbecue sauce, Mumbo, for a South Side restaurant; WETA's Boundary Stones dates the trademark to 1958 and the family's Chicago restaurants to the 1940s, and the Mumbo mark was registered federally in 1999 by his successor Select Brands. Whether Chicago mild sauce and D.C. mumbo sauce are the same thing travelling, two things converging, or one thing renamed is exactly what neither the trademark record nor the food writing settles.

*Inference —* the shacks' bulletproof-glass counters, which Wikipedia describes as a necessity rather than a design choice at Harold's, shaped the food: everything in this style survives being handed through a slot in a box.
text.how: Cut the wing, flour it lightly or not at all, and fry it hard — longer and darker than a Buffalo wing, until the skin has no give. Lay white bread in the bottom of the box, fries on the bread, wings on the fries. Pour mild sauce over the top, or ask for it on the side and pour it yourself. Recipes vary shop to shop and are not published; the ATK account describes tomato paste and ketchup with sugar, vinegar, cayenne, mustard powder and garlic powder. Many houses also pour hot, and many customers order half mild and half hot.
text.today: Harold's had over 100 locations as of 2025, including three in Atlanta and one in Charlotte, and the chain's daughter-of-the-founder CEO Kristen Pierce died in January 2026. Mild sauce is bottled by several makers and sold on shelves. The question of who owns a sauce that a neighbourhood invented is live: WETA's account of the parallel D.C. fight records a petition arguing mumbo had become generic "like aspirin" and a Trademark Trial and Appeal Board ruling that the evidence did not prove it.

kin.as: The sauce itself — ketchup and tomato paste, sugar, vinegar, cayenne — poured over the whole box rather than tossed with the wings.

A barbecue sauce is brushed or tossed and tastes of smoke and molasses. Mild sauce is thinner, tangier, blunter, and it gets poured over the box.

names.name: Mumbo sauce wings
names.said: Spelled mumbo on one plexiglass menu board and mambo on the next, in the same neighbourhood, for the same sauce.

text.what: Fried chicken wings, usually whole and uncut, sold through the window of a Washington carryout and drowned in mumbo sauce — red, sweeter than barbecue sauce and by turns sharper or more sour, depending whose kitchen made it. The same sauce goes on french fries, fried jumbo shrimp and fried rice, and the wings-over-fried-rice box is the form the dish most often takes across the D.C., Maryland and Virginia carryouts. The sauce arrives poured, not tossed, and the container it comes in is styrofoam.
text.story:
Two cities claim the sauce and the record does not hand it to either cleanly.

The Chicago side has the paperwork. Argia B. Collins Sr. carried a family recipe from Mississippi to Chicago in the 1940s and opened barbecue restaurants on the South Side with his brothers, selling a sauce they called mumbo; WETA's Boundary Stones dates his trademark to 1958, and his bottled sauce reached grocery wholesalers by November 1968 and came in mild, tangy and hickory by 1970. His successor Select Brands registered the Mumbo mark federally on 25 May 1999, and has challenged D.C. uses of the name as infringement.

The Washington side has the neighbourhood. Boundary Stones puts mumbo in D.C. carryouts "at least since the 1960s" — Black-owned first, then Asian-owned — and says outright: "Origin stories vary so it is difficult to say for sure who introduced Mumbo sauce to the District." Wings 'N Things at 7th and Florida NW is the name most often given; Johnny Boy in Capitol Heights, Maryland is another. Capital City Mumbo Sauce dates the D.C. sauce to a restaurant called Wings-n-Things in the late 1960s.

And a third thread runs through Buffalo. John Young sold breaded whole wings in a tomato sauce he called mumbo at John Young's Wings 'n Things in Buffalo from 1961 — and credited a Washington, D.C. restaurant as where he heard of the idea, by way of a travelling boxer who told him a D.C. place was doing good business in wings. Because Collins's Chicago sauce predates all of it, Wikipedia records the speculation that D.C.'s is a transplanted Chicago sauce; it also records that the Trademark Trial and Appeal Board, after two years, found a D.C. company could not take the name from its Chicago founder. Arsha Jones, who launched Capital City Mumbo Sauce in May 2011, had argued the word had gone generic in D.C. "like aspirin"; the board ruled the evidence insufficient and her company became Capital City Mambo Sauce.

The city argues about it in public. In 2018 Mayor Muriel Bowser called mumbo sauce "annoying" in a Facebook post and questioned whether it was "quintessential" D.C.; her spokesperson said the remarks were meant to liven up Thanksgiving. McDonald's put out its own version as a limited offering on 9 October 2023 with a short documentary attached.
text.how: Fry the wing whole and hard at a carryout fryer — jointed wings show up, but the uncut whole wing is the D.C. shape. Build the box: fried rice or fries at the bottom, wings on top. Pour the mumbo over, or ask for it in a cup. The sauce is ketchup-forward, sweet, with vinegar and heat behind it; every carryout runs its own, and no two are the same thickness. There is no toss and no dip on the side unless you buy one.
text.today: Mumbo is bottled by more than one company and sold in grocery stores, and the go-go band Mambo Sauce, a Christylez Bacon song, a Black Flag Brewing beer, a Camille Acker short story and an event series called Chicken & Mumbo Sauce all take their names from it. *Inference —* the wing-and-mumbo box outlived the argument about who owns the word, because the carryout counter never asked.

kin.as: The sauce this style is entirely about, and the thing two cities and a trademark board have fought over.

names.name: Garlic parmesan wings
names.said: Abbreviated on nearly every board that sells it: garlic parm, two words, no capitals.

text.what: A fried wing tossed in melted butter or oil with garlic and grated parmesan, often with dried herbs and black pepper, sometimes finished with more cheese out of the bowl so it sits in visible flecks. It carries no chile heat, which is the point: it is the order placed by the person at the table who does not want heat, and it sells beside Buffalo rather than against it. Some kitchens pour it as a sauce, some dust dry cheese onto a buttered wing, and the two versions eat differently — one slick, one powdery.
text.story:
The origin is not established, and this record does not supply one.

What the sources searched here give is a shape rather than a story. Garlic and parmesan on fried chicken is Italian-American ground, and the wing itself grew up in Italian-American bars and pizzerias — the Anchor Bar was a Bellissimo family business, the wings went out with celery and blue cheese off an antipasto tray, and Buffalo's pizzerias sold wings alongside pies. *Inference —* garlic parm looks like a pizzeria's ingredients applied to a bar's dish. That is a reading of where the ingredients already were, not a documented invention, and this project names no inventor, no restaurant and no year.

The dating evidence that exists is negative and thin. A 2015 consumer survey by Ask Your Target Market put barbecue at 43 percent, mild Buffalo at 30, hot Buffalo at 24 and plain at 14, and folded garlic parmesan into an "other" category at 9 percent alongside teriyaki. The National Chicken Council's Super Bowl wing round-up listed Wingstop's top flavours as Original Hot, Lemon Pepper and Hickory Smoked BBQ, with no garlic parmesan among them. Trade writing since has ranked garlic parmesan among the country's most-ordered flavours; this project could not retrieve a primary national ranking to cite for that, so the claim that it has become a top-two or top-three flavour stays unverified here.

*Inference —* the rise is easier to see on menus than in surveys. Jeremiah's Tavern in Rochester, read on 16 September 2026, listed Garlic Parm among sixteen sauces; every national wing chain carries a version.
text.how: Fry the wing bare and hot, so the skin is dry enough to take fat without going soft. Melt butter with minced or granulated garlic — raw garlic burns and turns bitter, so most kitchens cook it in the butter first or use powder. Toss the wings through it. Add grated parmesan into the bowl for the sauced version, or dust it onto the buttered wings for the dry one; a hard cheese melts into strings if it goes in too hot, which is why some houses add it off the heat. Dried oregano, parsley and cracked pepper are common. Ranch usually goes on the side, and blue cheese fights the cheese already on the wing.
text.today: Garlic parm is on the board at essentially every chain and independent wing counter in the United States, in bottled form on grocery shelves, and in a dry-seasoning version for air fryers and party packs. It also turns up as a half order — half Buffalo, half parm — which is how a table that disagrees about heat resolves it.

names.name: Korean fried chicken wings
names.said: Order half and half — yangnyeom ban, huraideu ban — and the box comes divided down the middle.

text.what: Chicken fried twice so the crust comes out thin and brittle — Julia Moskin of The New York Times called it "thin, crackly and almost transparent" — then hand-painted with sauce by brush rather than shaken in a bowl, so the coating stays a thin film and the crust keeps its snap. Two sauces carry the style: yangnyeom, sweet and spicy on a gochujang base, and ganjang, soy and sugar and a great deal of garlic. Wings and drums arrive whole or jointed depending on the house. Pickled radish comes in a tub alongside, and beer with it; the pairing has its own word, chimaek, from chicken and maekju.
text.story:
Frying chicken is old in Korea — a fifteenth-century method survives, and an early Joseon dish called pogye was cooked in oil with soy sauce, sesame oil, flour-and-water and vinegar poured in turn. The modern chain runs from the late 1960s, when Myeongdong Yeongyang Center in Seoul sold whole chicken roasted over an electric oven. U.S. military presence after the Korean War introduced deep-fried chicken; cooking oil did not become widely available until the 1970s. Lims Chicken, the first modern franchise, opened in 1977 in the basement of the Shinsegae department store on Chungmu-ro, founded by Yu Seok-ho, and was taken up as a pairing for draft beer.

Yangnyeom has a date and a reason. Yun Jonggye, running a fried chicken restaurant in Daegu in 1982, noticed customers struggling with the hard crisp shell — scraped palates among the complaints — and marinated the chicken sweet and spicy to soften it. Kentucky Fried Chicken opened in South Korea in 1984. The Asian financial crisis of the late 1990s pushed laid-off workers into opening chicken shops, and the count kept climbing: over 20,000 restaurants by 2013, 36,000 by 2017, 40,000 as of 2026, with 1,800 more run abroad by Korean brands in 60 countries — double the figure of ten years earlier. Almost a third of the chicken eaten in South Korea is fried.

The American side arrived through those brands. Bonchon, founded by Jinduk Seo in Busan in 2002, opened its first U.S. location in Fort Lee, New Jersey, built the business on a double-fry method and two centrally manufactured sauces — soy garlic and spicy — and closed its South Korean retail operations by the end of 2016 to franchise abroad. It now runs about 500 restaurants in more than ten countries, with more than 150 in the U.S. generating over 60 percent of worldwide revenue, and moved its global headquarters to Dallas in 2021. Mexicana, Kyochon, Genesis BBQ, Pelicana and Nene followed the same route out.

*Inference —* the style met the American wing market halfway. A cuisine that sells whole birds and boneless sunsal in Korea sells wings and drums in the United States, because that is the cut an American bar menu is built around.
text.how: Cut or leave whole, season before frying — spices, sugar and salt go on both before and after — and fry once at a lower heat to cook it through, rest it, then fry again hot to drive off moisture and set a thin shell. Smaller or medium birds, which give more tender meat. Brush the sauce on in a thin even layer rather than tossing, or leave it plain as huraideu. Yangnyeom for sweet-and-spicy, ganjang for soy-garlic, banban for half of each. Serve with pickled radish cubes and beer or a carbonated drink.
text.today: Korean chains run across 21 U.S. states and Bonchon was one of the few restaurant groups still adding stores through the COVID-19 pandemic. Its owner VIG Partners put the brand up for auction in March 2026; the process drew over 100 potential buyers from the United States and Asia. The National Chicken Council's Super Bowl LX note, dated 28 January 2026, listed Korean barbecue among the global flavours moving into American wing menus.

names.name: Memphis dry-rub wings
names.said: Dry or wet is the first question at a Memphis counter, and it is asked about ribs before it is asked about wings.

text.what: A wing finished with the rub that Memphis puts on ribs — salt and a spice blend, house by house, usually paprika-led — and handed over without sauce. The city's rib counters run the dry-and-wet split: dry means rubbed before cooking and eaten as is, wet means brushed with sauce before, during and after. The wing borrows the split whole. It comes off a smoker at some houses, out of a fryer at others, and off both at a few, and the rub goes on at the end either way so the seasoning stays granular instead of dissolving.
text.story:
Memphis barbecue is a pork tradition with a documented vocabulary and a long bench of rib houses — Charlie Vergos' Rendezvous from 1948, Interstate Bar-B-Que from 1978, Neely's from 1988, Central BBQ from 2002. Chicken and beef sit on those menus beside the ribs and the shoulder, and Central BBQ's smoked chicken wings are named in the record of the style.

The wing's own scene is younger and better documented as a scene than as a history. The Memphis Flyer, surveying eight wing experiences in the city in March 2021, found wings "in trucks, in stores, in outlet malls, even in gas stations" and ran through D'Bo's Wings 'n More — started with a dream and a trailer in 1990 — along with Uncle Lou's, Riko's Kickin' Chicken, India Palace, Habee's Wings & Deli, The Wing Guru, Ching's Hot Wings and Belmont Grill, which the piece dates to adding wings around 1987 or 1988. Habee's calls its dry version "Dry heat", and the Flyer's writer liked it for the texture: crunchier skin, tender meat, no glaze.

*Inference —* the dry wing in Memphis is the rib counter's habit applied to a cheaper bird, not a separate invention. This project found no source naming a first dry-rub wing, a cook or a year, and none is claimed here.
text.how: Two routes, and both end the same way. Off the pit: rub, smoke low until the skin tightens, then dust again with the same rub going out — some houses run the wings hot at the end, over direct heat or through the fryer, to fix the skin. Out of the fryer: fry bare and hard, then toss in the rub while the surface is hot enough to hold it. Either way the rub goes on last and stays dry. Sauce, if anybody wants it, arrives in a cup on the side. Rub recipes are house property and are not published; the record on Memphis rubs says only that they are salt and various spices.
text.today: Memphis wing counters carry dry alongside lemon pepper, hot and the honey-gold sauces the city's shops are known for, so the dry order is one line on a long board rather than the whole menu. Central BBQ ships and appears nationally on television. *Inference —* dry travels badly on a delivery app, where a sauce photographs and a dust does not, which is part of why the style stayed local while Nashville's went everywhere.

names.name: Nashville hot wings
names.said: The heat levels are the menu: plain, mild, medium, hot, and whatever the house calls the one above that.

text.what: Hot chicken's method put on a wing: marinate in a water- or buttermilk-based seasoned blend, flour, fry, then paint with a cayenne paste loosened with fat drawn from the fryer. The paste stains the crust deep red and goes on with a spoon and gloved hands, then gets squeezed in. It lands on white bread with pickle chips — the bread catching the grease, the pickles cutting it — and the bread is part of the dish, not a napkin. Heat runs in named steps and the top step is genuinely punishing.
text.story:
Anecdotal evidence puts spicy fried chicken in Nashville's African American communities for generations, perhaps from the 1930s, while the current style of spice paste may date only to the mid-1970s. The origin generally accepted belongs to the family of André Prince Jeffries, who has run Prince's Hot Chicken Shack since 1980; before that it was her great-uncle Thornton Prince's.

The story she tells is an accident. Thornton was, by the family's account, a womanizer; after a late Saturday night his girlfriend cooked him a fried chicken breakfast loaded with pepper as revenge. He liked it, and by the mid-1930s he and his brothers had a recipe and a café, the BBQ Chicken Shack. Wikipedia's article on the restaurant notes the story is impossible to verify.

The café started at 28th and Jefferson, moved downtown into Hell's Half Acre near the Ryman Auditorium, and drew Opry stars after performances — under segregation, with a separate room built at the back for white guests, reached by walking through the main dining room and the kitchen. Thornton's brother Will took over when he died, Will's wife Maude ran it after him, and in 1980 Maude decided the business should go to Thornton's great-niece, who dropped the BBQ from the name. The shop moved to Ewing Drive in East Nashville in 1988. In December 2018 a Ford Explorer crashed into the Ewing Drive strip mall and set it on fire; the restaurant itself was undamaged, but building damage and landlord delays turned a two-week closure into a permanent one seven months later.

*Inference —* the wing is a later cut than the dish. Hot chicken is a breast, thigh or wing quarter in its standard description, and the wing-only plate reads as the method following the market for wings rather than the other way round.

The method left town fast. Bill Purcell, Nashville's former mayor, sponsored the Music City Hot Chicken Festival and called his table at Prince's his "second office". By 2015 about two dozen Nashville restaurants served it. KFC put Nashville Hot Chicken and Nashville Hot Tenders on U.S. menus in January 2016 after a Pittsburgh trial it called the most successful product testing in its recent history, and ran it in the UK from 22 May to 18 June 2017. Buffalo Wild Wings sells a Nashville-hot-style wing. Prince's was named an American Classic by the James Beard Foundation in 2013.
text.how: Marinate the wings — nearly all hot chicken goes into buttermilk, for flavour and to keep the meat from drying in the oil. Flour them. Fry, in a pan at most houses rather than a deep fryer, though pressure fryers and deep fryers both get used. Make the paste: cayenne first, sometimes sugar, garlic or extra hot sauce, loosened with fat lifted out of the frying oil so it goes on hot and clings. Traditional order is paste after the fryer; some kitchens paste before breading and fry again. Spoon it on, squeeze it in. Serve on white bread with pickles. Recipes and heat steps are house secrets and are not published.
text.today: Hot chicken restaurants run in Atlanta, New York, Philadelphia, Chicago, Los Angeles, Birmingham, Louisville, Ann Arbor, Columbus, Salt Lake City and Seattle, and abroad in Calgary, Seoul and Melbourne. Chains built on the style include Hattie B's, Dave's Hot Chicken, Howlin' Ray's, Angry Chickz, Joella's and World Famous Hotboys. Hattie B's, founded by a father and son both named Nick Bishop, opened in Midtown Nashville on 9 August 2012, uses ghost peppers in its hottest step, and opened its first Midwestern location in Chicago's Wrigleyville in 2026.

names.name: Rochester breaded wings
names.said: Order in Rochester and the counter asks which sauce, not how hot. Country Sweet is a sauce, a brand and an answer.

text.what: A chicken wing dredged in seasoned flour before it goes in the oil, fried until the coating sets hard, then glazed rather than tossed loose — most often in Country Sweet, a sweet-and-tangy sauce a Rochester kitchen built in 1977 that is neither barbecue nor cayenne-and-butter. Breading is the whole argument: seventy miles west, Buffalo puts the wing in the fryer bare. Rochester bars also pour plain cayenne sauce, barbecue, teriyaki and garlic parmesan, so a breaded wing is a coating rather than a single flavour.
text.story:
Country Sweet dates itself to 1977, when Tom Lask worked up a sauce in a Rochester home kitchen; the company's own account calls it neither barbecue nor Buffalo. It sells the sauce in mild, hot and BBQ, and sells the wings hand-breaded. That is the firmest dated fact this project could find for the style.

Everything around it is thin. No published history of Rochester's breaded wing turned up in the sources searched here — no founder, no first bar, no year. The city's documented food identity runs elsewhere: the Garbage Plate, trademarked by Nick Tahou Hots and traced to 1918, and the Zweigle's white hot. Wings sit underneath that, carried by menus rather than by writing about menus.

*Tradition holds —* a half-and-half order comes half in the sweet sauce and half in hot, and a 'hot plate' means the wings and the sides under one pour. This project found no published source describing either, so both stay unverified here.

The rivalry gets stated in print even where the history does not. CITY Magazine, naming Jeremiah's Tavern the city's best wings, wrote: "It's easy to find really good wings on damn near every corner in Buffalo. Around here? A little more challenging."
text.how: Dredge the cut wing in seasoned flour — some shops dip in buttermilk or egg first, some go dry — and drop it in the oil. The coating browns into a shell that holds sauce on its surface instead of soaking it in, which is why a sweet glaze works here and slides off a bare Buffalo wing. Fry, then glaze: Country Sweet goes on as a sticky coat rather than a loose toss in a bowl. Blue cheese and celery come alongside, same as west of here. A tavern that fries bare will say so on the board; breaded and naked both sell in this city.
text.today: Country Sweet runs shops in Rochester and Greece and bottles the sauce for grocery shelves. Bar menus carry long sauce lists beside the house breading: Jeremiah's Tavern, read on 16 September 2026, offered sixteen sauces including Garlic Parm, Cajun Dry Rub, Jamaican Jerk and Korean BBQ, with ten traditional wings at $17.99 and twelve boneless at $16.00. *Inference —* the breading, not the sauce, is what makes the plate legible as Rochester's; the sauce list is the same list every American wing counter now prints.

names.name: Smoked barbecue wings
names.said: A pit sells wings the way it sells everything else — by the pound, off the same fire, at the same window.

text.what: A wing cooked on a barbecue pit rather than in oil: rubbed, smoked over wood until the fat renders, then finished — brushed with a tomato sauce and set over higher heat to tack up, or dropped briefly in the fryer so the skin crisps. Regional sauce follows regional pit. Kansas City runs thick tomato sauces; Memphis runs the dry-and-wet split; Texas leans on the rub and the wood. The wing is a side item on those menus, cooked with the ribs and the shoulder and sold beside them.
text.story:
American barbecue's regional map is old and well drawn, and the wing arrived on it late. The pits and their dates are documented — Charlie Vergos' Rendezvous in Memphis from 1948, Interstate Bar-B-Que from 1978, Neely's from 1988, Central BBQ from 2002 — and the chicken sits on those menus beside beef and pork. Central BBQ's smoked chicken wings are named in the record of Memphis barbecue, which is one of the few places a smoked wing gets recorded as a menu item at all.

Kansas City is the thick-tomato pole; Gates Bar-B-Q is noted for a spicier version built on cumin and celery salt. Texas splits four ways: East Texas by way of the Southern tradition, Central Texas out of German and Czech butcher shops, West Texas over mesquite with goat and mutton, South Texas barbacoa from a cow's head. Alabama's contribution is the pale sauce: chicken smoked in the pit and then coated or dunked in Bob Gibson's white sauce.

*Inference —* the smoked wing is the pit's answer to the sports-bar wing, not an older tradition with its own history. This project found no source dating a first barbecue-joint wing or naming the pit that started it, and none is asserted.

*Tradition holds —* the finishing step exists because smoke alone leaves wing skin slack, and a pit that wants a wing to eat like a wing puts heat on it at the end.
text.how: Rub the wings and hold them. Smoke at low heat over wood — hickory through the South, oak and mesquite in Texas — until the fat has rendered and the meat pulls. Then make a decision: brush with sauce and put the wings back over direct heat until the sugar tacks and darkens, or drop them in hot oil for a minute to tighten the skin and sauce them after. Sauce goes on at the end either way, because a tomato sauce with sugar in it burns over a long cook. A dry finish — rub again, no sauce — makes it a Memphis dry wing instead.
text.today: Barbecue restaurants ship, franchise and appear on television, and the smoked wing travels with them. Home smokers and pellet grills put the method in back yards, where it competes with the fryer and the air fryer for the same bird. *Inference —* what a pit sells as a wing is a cheaper cut of the same labour: hours of wood for a piece that a fryer turns out in ten minutes.

names.name: Alabama white sauce
names.said: A tub of it goes on the table in north Alabama the way a red sauce does everywhere else.

text.what: A mayonnaise-based barbecue sauce, thin, pale and sharp. Typical ingredients are vinegar, lemon juice, salt, pepper, cayenne pepper and horseradish stirred into mayonnaise. It goes on barbecue chicken, which is an Alabama speciality, and on wings — dunked whole rather than brushed.
text.story:
White sauce was invented in Decatur, Alabama in 1925. It is believed to have been made by Bob Gibson at Big Bob Gibson Bar-B-Q there.

Alabama barbecue centres on pork cooked in open pits over hickory, with oak and pecan also used. A vinegar-based sauce like North Carolina's is common in the north of the state; a tomato-based one is usual south of Birmingham. White sauce stayed a north Alabama thing until 1994, when it began to be bottled and sold commercially.

Barbecue became popular in Alabama in the early 19th century, with roots in Native American cooking. Local militias held barbecues to get members to turn up for yearly drills, and they served as political and civic gatherings; by the late 1820s some social reformers opposed them, arguing they encouraged "political debasement" or that the alcohol and merrymaking were a moral problem. They failed. The first barbecue restaurants opened in the 1890s; the oldest continuously operating one in the state is Golden Rule Bar-B-Q, founded in 1891. In 2015 the Alabama Department of Tourism ran "The Year of Alabama Barbecue".
text.how: Dunk, do not brush. A whole smoked or fried chicken goes into the tub and comes out coated; wings go in by the basket. Mayonnaise splits over direct heat, so the sauce meets the bird after the fire, not during. It doubles as a dressing for the slaw beside it.
text.today: Bottled since 1994 and now sold nationally by several Alabama makers. As of 16 September 2026 the USDA label panel for Saw's Alabama White Sauce reads 300 mg sodium, 1 g sugar and 17 g fat in a 2-tablespoon serving — 150 mg and 0.5 g in one tablespoon, with soybean oil first and two vinegars on the list. Big Bob Gibson's own bottle returns no record in FoodData Central, so its panel is not on this disk. Nobody publishes a Scoville number.

names.name: Blue cheese dressing
names.said: In Buffalo it arrives without being ordered. Asking for ranch instead is noticed.

text.what: A thick white dip of blue cheese with mayonnaise and buttermilk, sour cream or yogurt, plus milk, vinegar, onion powder and garlic powder. A vinaigrette version exists — salad oil, blue cheese, vinegar and seasonings — and is not what comes with wings. Sold by most major dressing makers in the United States and Canada, and served as the dip beside Buffalo wings and raw vegetables.
text.story:
It reached the wing on the first night, if the Anchor Bar's account holds: Teressa Bellissimo sent the wings out with celery and blue cheese taken off the bar's antipasto tray. Whether that was 1964 is one of the arguments the origin carries.

What is not argued is which dip Buffalo uses. The standard description of a Buffalo wing gives blue cheese or ranch; the same source records that ranch is the most popular wing dip in the United States. Buffalo's own bars serve blue cheese.

The dip has a chemistry problem the argument ignores. Water and oil separate in it — an unstable emulsion — and salad dressings spoil through organisms like Saccharomyces bailii and Lactobacillus fructivorans, the latter an acid-tolerant facultative anaerobe that survives the low pH a blue cheese dressing sits at.

*Inference —* the chunks are the point. A smooth blue cheese dressing and a chunky one taste alike on a spoon and do not behave alike on a wing, because the chunks survive the dip and the smooth part does not.
text.how: Cold, in a cup, beside the wing — never poured over it. A wing goes in, comes out with a load of cheese, and the celery goes in after to clear the palate. Home versions whisk mayonnaise, buttermilk and sour cream with lemon juice or vinegar and fold blue cheese in at the end, cubed rather than crumbled so some of it stays in pieces.
text.today: On every wing plate in western New York and in the dip section of every wing chain. As of 16 September 2026 the USDA label panel for Ken's Steak House Chunky Blue Cheese Dressing reads 290 mg sodium, 13 g fat and 1 g sugar in a 2-tablespoon serving — 145 mg and 0.5 g in one tablespoon. Soybean oil is first; blue cheese is fourth, behind water and vinegar.

recipes.author: Wikibooks Cookbook contributors
ingredients: 2 tbsp (30 ml) lemon juice or vinegar (cider or white wine)

Pour the mayonnaise mixture into a serving container and stir in the cubes and crumbs of cheese.

names.name: Buffalo sauce
names.said: Nobody in a Buffalo kitchen calls it Buffalo sauce. It is the sauce, and you order it by heat: mild, medium, hot.

text.what: Cayenne pepper hot sauce cut with melted butter. Two things, warmed together and held warm, poured over fried wings in a metal bowl and shaken. More butter reads mild, less reads hot, and a kitchen moves between the three by changing that ratio rather than the pepper. Worcestershire sauce and garlic powder turn up in plenty of versions. Bottled ready-to-use wing sauce does the same job with oil and butter flavouring in place of butter, because butter separates on a shelf.
text.story:
Cayenne pepper sauce arrived in Buffalo in a bottle. Frank's RedHot came out of Cincinnati and a Louisiana pepper farm in 1920; Crystal came out of New Orleans in 1923. Neither was made for wings.

The sauce got its name in 1964, or later, depending on whose account you take. At the Anchor Bar, Teressa Bellissimo fried wings and tossed them in cayenne sauce; the Bellissimo family told three different versions of that night, and Dominic Bellissimo gave Calvin Trillin one of them in 1980. John Young was selling breaded whole wings in a tomato-based mumbo sauce in Buffalo from 1961, and said the Anchor Bar did not carry wings as a regular menu item until 1974.

*Inference —* the butter is the part that travelled least well. A wing tossed at the counter gets butter; a wing that has to survive a shelf, a delivery bag or a factory gets oil and a butter flavouring. Frank's RedHot Buffalo Wings Sauce lists canola oil fifth and natural butter type flavour eighth, with no butter on the label.

Wikipedia's article on the wing notes that Frank's RedHot "was probably not the hot sauce that was used in the original 1964 Anchor Bar recipe." Nobody has produced the bottle.
text.how: Melt butter. Stir in cayenne pepper sauce off the heat and keep the mix warm, not hot, so it does not split. Fry the wings, drain them a moment, drop them in a bowl, pour the sauce over and shake — sauce after the fryer, never before, or the coating steams instead of sticking. Ratio sets the heat: roughly equal parts reads mild, more sauce than butter reads hot. Add Worcestershire sauce, garlic powder or a little vinegar if the house does.
text.today: Sold bottled by every large sauce maker and by most bars as house-made. The bottled kind states its heat on the front; the house kind states it at the counter. Nobody publishes a Scoville figure — the capsaicin measure named for the chemist Wilbur Scoville — for a finished Buffalo sauce, because the butter ratio changes it batch to batch. As of 16 September 2026, the USDA label panel for Frank's RedHot Buffalo Wings Sauce reads 460 mg sodium and no sugar in a tablespoon.

text.what: A reddish-orange Louisiana pepper sauce made by Baumer Foods since 1923: aged red cayenne peppers, distilled vinegar, salt. Three ingredients on the 6 fl oz bottle; the gallon jug adds xanthan gum. Writers put it against Tabasco as having "a more prominent dark chile flavor, and a slightly subdued vinegar profile". Buffalo kitchens that do not buy Frank's usually buy this.
text.story:
Baumer Foods started in New Orleans and stayed a family business. Its factory on Tulane Avenue in Mid-City carried a lighted sign — a chef stirring a pot, steam from the plant venting out through the pot — visible from Interstate 10 and known across the city. The preserves the sign advertised went into US military rations in the Second World War and are no longer made.

Hurricane Katrina wrecked much of the New Orleans plant in 2005, sign included. The company moved production up the Mississippi to Reserve, in St. John the Baptist Parish; the sign was replicated and set on top of a new apartment building on the old factory site. As of April 2021 the head office sits in Metairie.

Three million US gallons a year ship to seventy-five countries. The brand is popular in Saudi Arabia, carried there by Louisiana petroleum workers. David Chang has said Crystal is his favourite hot sauce, and Ed Currie, who bred the Carolina Reaper, called it "probably the best tasting of the table sauces."
text.how: Same job as any cayenne bottle: melt butter, stir the sauce in warm, toss fried wings in it. *Tradition holds —* cooks who choose Crystal over Frank's say it needs a touch less butter, because the vinegar sits further back. It is also the pepper sauce that goes into a Nashville paste, into gumbo and onto eggs.
text.today: Made in Reserve, Louisiana; head office in Metairie. As of 16 September 2026 the USDA label panel for the 6 fl oz bottle reads 135 mg sodium in a 1 teaspoon serving — 405 mg in a tablespoon — with no sugar. Baumer publishes no Scoville number, which is the usual case: almost no wing-sauce maker does.

names.name: Frank's RedHot
aliases: Frank's RedHot Original Cayenne Pepper Sauce
names.said: A bar orders it by the case and says 'Frank's' the way it says 'a Coke'.

text.what: A thin orange cayenne pepper sauce: aged cayenne red peppers, distilled vinegar, water, salt, garlic powder, in that order on the label. McCormick & Company makes it. The Original blend measures 450 Scoville heat units — the capsaicin scale named for Wilbur Scoville — which puts it below Tabasco, Cholula and Tapatío, and barely above Sriracha; the XTRA Hot blend measures 2,000. It is the bottle most Buffalo wing recipes start from.
text.story:
Jacob Frank founded the Frank Tea and Spice Company in Cincinnati, Ohio in 1896. In 1917 he contracted with the Estilette Pepper Farm in Louisiana and went into partnership with Adam Estilette. They mixed spices, vinegar, garlic and cayenne peppers, aged them, and put the blend on the market in 1920.

Ownership moved: Durkee Famous Foods in 1977, Reckitt Benckiser from 1995, and in August 2017 McCormick & Company closed a $4.2 billion deal that took in both French's mustard and Frank's RedHot. Production sits in Springfield, Missouri.

The wing connection is older than the ownership and thinner than the marketing. Wikipedia's Buffalo wing article says Frank's "was probably not the hot sauce that was used in the original 1964 Anchor Bar recipe." *Inference —* the bottle's grip on the wing was won after the fact, by being cheap, thin, and everywhere.

The brand's television campaign gave it a second life: an elderly woman named Ethel, planted in front of a dignitary, says of her recipes "I put that s*** on everything", bleeped, with a splat over her mouth.
text.how: Shake. Pour into melted butter for wings, roughly one part to one for mild, more sauce for hot. Straight on eggs, pizza, fried chicken, and into chili. The vinegar is the working part as much as the pepper: it cuts fat and it keeps the sauce thin enough to coat rather than cling.

recipes.text:
Break up half a dozen red peppers. Add three dozen black peppercorns and two tablespoonfuls of sugar to a quart of vinegar. Scald vinegar and sugar, and pour over the peppers. Put in a jar, steep eight hours, strain and bottle.

This is to be eaten with fish or raw oysters.

names.name: Garlic parmesan sauce
names.said: 'Garlic parm' at the counter. Half the shops mean a creamy sauce, half mean butter and a dry cheese shake, and the menu rarely says which.

text.what: A pale, garlicky wing coating with parmesan in it. Two versions share the name: a creamy emulsified sauce built on oil and egg yolk with parmesan powder, sold bottled; and a kitchen mix of melted butter, minced garlic and grated parmesan tossed over the wings and finished with more cheese and parsley. Neither has heat in it. Both leave the wing wet and the fingers cheesy.
text.story:
Garlic parm belongs to the sauce-board era. As the market for chicken wings expanded, restaurants began creating and using sauces beyond Buffalo, and a wing menu turned into a list — Wingstop carries thirteen wing sauces, some running only for a marketing window, and sells ranch, blue cheese, honey mustard and cheese sauce as dips beside them.

*Inference —* garlic parm is the wing answer to garlic bread, which is crusty bread topped with garlic and butter and sometimes cheese, then toasted. A kitchen that already had butter, garlic and a tub of grated parmesan did not need a new ingredient to add a flavour to the board.

The sauce splits the same way lemon pepper does: dry shake or wet sauce. The bottled version settles the argument by emulsifying, so the cheese stays suspended and the sauce keeps on a shelf.
text.how: Melt butter with minced or roasted garlic, off the heat so the garlic does not brown. Toss the fried wings in it, then shower grated parmesan and chopped parsley over the top while the butter is still wet enough to hold them. The bottled sauce skips the melting: it pours cold and clings, because oil and egg yolk hold it together.
text.today: On the board at every wing chain and most bars. As of 16 September 2026 the USDA label panel for Kinder's Garlic Parmesan Wing Sauce & Dip reads 120 mg sodium and 1 g sugar in a 1-tablespoon serving — the lowest sodium of any bottled wing sauce measured for this set — with soybean oil first and roasted garlic puree second. No Scoville number is published, and the label names no chile.

names.name: Honey barbecue sauce
names.said: The order a table puts in for the person who does not want heat, and the one children get.

text.what: A thick sweet red sauce: corn syrup or sugar, vinegar, tomato, honey, smoke flavour and spices. Sticky enough to hold on a wing without butter, sweet enough to caramelise under a broiler or on a grill. Every wing chain sells one, and it is usually the mildest thing on the board.
text.story:
Barbecue sauce reached the wing through the pizza chains. Domino's added Buffalo wings to its national menu in 1994 after four Super Bowl appearances by the Buffalo Bills, and Pizza Hut followed the next year. As the market grew, restaurants built out sauces beyond Buffalo — some drawing on Chinese, Japanese, Thai, Caribbean and Indian cooking, some inventing combinations like Blueberry BBQ Wing Sauce or Maple/Bacon Glaze to hold customers' interest.

*Inference —* honey barbecue is the sauce that made a wing board possible. Once a menu had a second sauce it needed a sweet one, and every sauce added after that had somewhere to sit.

The sweet-and-sour tomato condiment behind it is much older than the wing: American home cookbooks were bottling a spiced 'chili sauce' of tomatoes, vinegar, sugar, onions and red peppers well before 1930.
text.how: Warm it — cold barbecue sauce slides off. Toss the fried wings in it, or brush it on a smoked or grilled wing in the last few minutes so the sugar sets without burning. It will burn: the sugar in it catches long before the skin is done, which is why it goes on at the end and never at the start.
text.today: On every wing board in America. As of 16 September 2026 the USDA label panel for Sweet Baby Ray's Honey Barbecue Sauce reads 300 mg sodium and 15 g sugar in a 2-tablespoon serving — 150 mg and 7.5 g in one tablespoon. High fructose corn syrup is its first ingredient; honey comes fourth, behind tomato paste. No Scoville number is published, and none would mean anything: the label declares no chile at all.

names.name: Hot honey
names.said: Drizzled, not tossed. A counter says 'hot honey' and reaches for a squeeze bottle.

text.what: Honey with chillies in it. Sweet first, then a heat that builds slowly — the flavour writers describe as "sweet-first" with a "slow-building heat". Goes on pizza, on fried chicken and wings, on roasted vegetables, with cheese, in sandwiches, on desserts, into glazes and marinades and dipping sauces, and into mixed drinks.
text.story:
Mixing honey with chillies has been done in many cultures for a long time. The American trend has a narrower start: Mike Kurtz encountered hot honey while studying in Brazil in 2004 and later founded Mike's Hot Honey, the brand the trend runs alongside.

It became a trend in early 2022, tracked by a steady rise in Google search interest, and spread through TikTok recipes. Business Insider named it a "new food obsession" in 2024. V8 and Tillamook among others released hot-honey snacks and product variations.

*Inference —* it reached the wing by way of the pizza it was already on. A kitchen with a squeeze bottle of it on the pass does not need a new ingredient to put a hot honey wing on the menu.
text.how: Drizzle it over the wings after they come out of the fryer, or brush it on at the end of a smoke or a grill so the sugar tightens without burning. It is thin enough to pour and thick enough to stay put. Plenty of kitchens use it as the second half of a Buffalo or Nashville wing rather than the whole coating, which is where the sweet-heat order comes from: pepper first, honey last.
text.today: Sold by dozens of makers, from national brands to single-state apiaries. As of 16 September 2026 the USDA label panel for Mike's Hot Honey reads three ingredients — honey, chilies, vinegar — with 0 mg sodium and 14 g sugar in a 1-tablespoon serving. Red Clay's version lists raw honey, apple cider vinegar and fermented habanero pepper at 15 g sugar and 10 mg sodium. No maker in this set publishes a Scoville number, and no chile is named by variety on the Mike's label.

names.name: Jerk marinade
names.said: One word covers three things: the rub, the wet marinade made from it, and the way of cooking. A jerk stand sells all three at once.

text.what: A wet marinade, or a dry rub, built on allspice and Scotch bonnet peppers — both native to Jamaica and grown there by the Taíno. Scallion, thyme, garlic, ginger, cloves, cinnamon, nutmeg, brown sugar, soy sauce, vinegar and salt turn up in it. The heat is the Scotch bonnet's. The word 'jerk' names the rub, the marinade and mop sauce made from it, and the cooking technique, all three.
text.story:
Jerking came from Jamaica's indigenous people, the Arawak and Taíno, and was taken up by the descendants of 17th-century Jamaican Maroons who lived among them. In 1516 the Spanish historian Gonzalo Fernández de Oviedo y Valdés recorded how the Taíno prepared and preserved meat and fish on a barbacoa, seasoning with native hot peppers — Scotch bonnet and cayenne — and pimento. Meats were sometimes wrapped in papaya leaves to tenderise before jerking. Local game went on it: coney, iguana, wild hog, agouti, wild birds, waterfowl, turtle, and a range of seafood.

Spanish colonists adopted Taíno methods to survive and introduced pig, cattle and chicken in the 1500s, curing them over a barbacoa with pimento wood and berries. When the Spanish were invaded in 1655 they freed the enslaved Africans, who fled into the countryside and became some of the first Jamaican Maroons; they intermingled with the remaining Taíno and learned jerking. By the end of the 18th century most groups had switched to imported pork, while the Maroons kept hunting wild hogs and jerking them.

The word comes from charqui, a Spanish term of Quechua origin for dried meat, which became 'jerky' in English.

Method followed portability. Around the 1960s Caribbean entrepreneurs began cutting oil barrels lengthwise, drilling ventilation holes and hinging lids to hold the smoke; the barrel drum is now standard across the island. Jerk stands sell the meat with hard dough bread, bammy, fried dumplings and festival.

Jerk travelled with the Caribbean diaspora — Britain, Canada, the United States, coastal Panama, Costa Rica, Honduras, Nicaragua, San Andrés. In September 2015 the Jamaican government registered Jamaica Jerk as a geographical indication, making Jamaica the first English-speaking Caribbean country to do so.
text.how: Marinate, then cook over smoke. Blend the wet version and work it under the skin; leave the wings in it for hours. Cook over pimento wood, in a halved oil drum with the lid down, or in a wood-burning oven; a home kitchen uses a grill and finishes in the fryer. Reserve some marinade unheated as a mop sauce and brush it on at the end. The Scotch bonnet's heat sits behind the allspice, which is the flavour people name first.
text.today: Sold bottled in every Caribbean grocery in the United States and in most supermarkets. As of 16 September 2026 the USDA label panel for Spur Tree Jamaican Jerk Seasoning reads 700 mg sodium and 1 g sugar in a 1-tablespoon serving, with scallion first and Scotch bonnet pepper second. No maker in this set publishes a Scoville number for it.

names.name: Lemon pepper
names.said: An Atlanta counter says 'lemon pepper' and means the dry shake; say 'wet' and you have ordered something else.

text.what: A dry blend of granulated lemon zest and cracked black peppercorns. The zest is mashed into the pepper so citrus oil soaks in, then the mix is baked and dried. Commercial blends add salt, sugar, onion powder, garlic powder, citric acid, lemon flavouring, sometimes cayenne. It started as a seafood seasoning and became the wing seasoning Atlanta is known for.
text.story:
William Shoffeitt, a product engineer in Healdsburg, California, launched lemon pepper seasoning commercially in July 1967 through his company, Shoffeitt's Enhance Seasoners. It sold along the West Coast, went out at food trade shows, and reached the shelves of Sears and JCPenney.

Atlanta made it a wing. Cooks there began adding lemon pepper to Buffalo wings to cut the heat, and the dry wing became emblematic of the city's food. Its mid-2000s run has been attributed to its not marking clothes the way an orange sauce does — a point made about rappers then wearing white t-shirts. Keisha Lance Bottoms, later mayor of Atlanta, said in 2017 that "Lemon pepper wings are Atlanta". Eric Kim wrote in The New York Times in 2022 that "in Atlanta, lemon pepper is queen".

*Inference —* the blend's move from fish counter to wing counter is the whole story of its second life, and the label never changed to follow it.
text.how: Shaken onto the wings straight out of the fryer, while the skin is hot enough to hold it. No sauce, no bowl — a dry wing stays crisp because nothing wet touches it. Some kitchens shake it over a wing that has already been through butter or Buffalo sauce, which is where wet begins.
text.today: On every supermarket spice shelf and behind every Atlanta wing counter. As of 16 September 2026 the USDA label panel for McCormick Lemon & Pepper Seasoning reads 180 mg sodium in a ¼-tablespoon serving — 720 mg in a whole tablespoon, which nobody eats. Salt is the first ingredient, ahead of the pepper; the lemon arrives as citric acid at 3 and lemon oil at 10.

names.name: Lemon pepper wet
names.said: Two words at the counter. 'Wet' means sauce underneath the shake, and for years at one Atlanta restaurant it was not on the menu at all.

text.what: A wing that has been through something wet and then through lemon pepper. The wet part varies: a lemon sauce instead of a dry rub at some shops, melted butter at others, Buffalo sauce at others again, with the dry seasoning shaken on after. American Deli in Atlanta invented the version the name usually points at.
text.story:
The dish reached most of America through television. The second episode of Atlanta shows a character handed "lemon pepper wet" wings from J.R. Crickets, a real Atlanta restaurant; the scene went round social media and the dish went with it. At the time J.R. Crickets did not have it on the menu — it had a similar item called "Fester" wings that customers kept calling lemon pepper wet. Writer Stephen Glover said he wanted the character "hooked up" with something that was not on the menu. The wings the show depicted were actually modelled on a dish from American Deli, a different Atlanta restaurant. J.R. Crickets added lemon pepper wet to its menu in 2017 in honour of the show. Mike Jordan of Eater Atlanta credited the episode with popularising it.

It kept collecting names. In 2020 Lou Williams of the Los Angeles Clippers picked up the nickname "Lemon Pepper Lou" after it was reported that he ordered lemon pepper wings with Jack Harlow at the Magic City strip club during a trip outside the NBA Bubble. Magic City already had a dish named for him, "Louwill Lemon Pepper BBQ Wings". He objected to the nickname and later trademarked it.

*Inference —* wet is the only wing order in America whose canonical version was invented by a customer, confirmed by a screenwriter, and then put on the menu by a restaurant that had not been serving it.
text.how: Fry the wings bare. Toss them in the wet part — lemon butter, plain melted butter, or Buffalo sauce — then shake dry lemon pepper over the top while the coating is still tacky. The order matters: shake first and it slides off; shake last and it sits on the surface where you taste it.
text.today: On Atlanta menus and, by 2026, on chain menus far from Atlanta. No maker bottles it, because it is not a bottle — it is a sequence. There is no label to read, no sodium figure, no Scoville number, and every shop's wet is a different wet.

names.name: Mango habanero
names.said: Sits near the top of a chain's heat ladder without being the top rung, which is usually something with a name like atomic.

text.what: A sweet-then-hot wing sauce: mango purée and corn syrup in front, habanero and cayenne behind. Orange, thick, and built to be tossed. It is the standard second-from-the-top rung on a chain wing board — hot enough to be a choice, sweet enough to finish.
text.story:
It belongs to the sauce-board era. As the market for chicken wings expanded, restaurants began creating and using a variety of sauces beyond Buffalo, some drawn from Chinese, Japanese, Thai, Caribbean and Indian cooking, and some invented as combinations — Blueberry BBQ Wing Sauce and Maple/Bacon Glaze among the examples — to hold customers' interest and grow the business.

Many bars and restaurants also build a deliberately extra-hot sauce for wing-eating challenges, and reward the people who finish with a photograph on the wall, a T-shirt, a free meal, or some combination.

*Inference —* mango habanero is the rung below that. It is where a board puts real heat that a table can still eat a whole basket of, which is why almost every chain carries a version and almost none of them publishes a number for it.
text.how: Toss, warm or cold — it is thick enough to cling without butter. Chains serve it on bone-in and boneless alike. A kitchen building its own reduces mango purée with vinegar and sugar and blends habanero in at the end, off the heat, because habanero's aroma cooks off before its heat does.
text.today: On chain boards nationally. As of 16 September 2026 the USDA label panel for Sweet Baby Ray's Mango Habanero Wing Sauce reads 100 mg sodium and 7 g sugar in a 1-tablespoon serving. Five chiles are named on that label — cayenne, habanero, chipotle, chili powder and chili de arbol — and no Scoville number is published for any of it, which is the pattern across this whole shelf.

names.name: Memphis dry rub
names.said: 'Dry' in Memphis is not a texture complaint. It is an order, and the other one is 'wet'.

text.what: A dry mix of salt, paprika, sugar and spices, patted onto meat before it cooks and shaken over it again after. Memphis barbecue is mostly pork — ribs and shoulders — and its ribs come dry or wet: dry means rub and no sauce, wet means sauce brushed on before, during and after. The same rub goes on wings, which get the rib counter's treatment without the pit.
text.story:
Memphis is one of the four regional styles of American barbecue usually named, with Carolina, Kansas City and Texas. Its cooking is slow, in a pit, and the dry-or-wet fork sits at the centre of it.

The World Championship Barbecue Cooking Contest, held each May, has made the style known beyond the city; Guinness World Records lists it as the largest pork barbecue contest in the world. The Food Network and the BBC cover it and more than 100,000 people attend. Many Memphis barbecue restaurants ship nationally overnight, helped by the FedEx Superhub sitting in the city.

*Inference —* the rub reached the wing sideways. A rib counter already had the mix in a shaker and a fryer or a smoker in the back, and a wing takes the same shake in a tenth of the time.
text.how: Two applications. Rub the wings before cooking so salt and sugar have time to draw and set a crust; smoke, fry or both; then shake more rub over them the moment they come off. The sugar is why a rubbed wing browns darker and why it will scorch on a hot grill. No bowl, no sauce, nothing to dip in unless you ask.
text.today: Sold bottled by dozens of makers and mixed by every barbecue kitchen. As of 16 September 2026 the USDA label panel for Adams Reserve Memphis Barbecue Rub reads 40 mg sodium and 1 g sugar in a ¼-teaspoon serving — 480 mg and 12 g in a tablespoon by arithmetic. Brown sugar is its first ingredient and chipotle its last. No Memphis rib house's own shaker carries a published panel, and no maker publishes a Scoville number.

kin.as: The style is this shaker, taken off the rib counter and put on a wing.
A Memphis pit whose rub goes on wings as well as ribs.

names.name: Mild sauce
names.said: 'Mild sauce on it' is a heat instruction nowhere else in America would read as a sauce order.

text.what: A red-brown condiment poured over fried chicken and wings on Chicago's South and West Sides. Recipes vary a great deal; many versions combine ketchup, barbecue sauce and hot sauce. Close kin to barbecue sauce and to mumbo sauce, and particularly associated with Black communities in Chicago. The name is not a heat rating — it is what the sauce is called.
text.story:
Fried chicken and barbecue restaurants made it: Harold's Chicken Shack, Uncle Remus Saucy Fried Chicken, Lem's Bar-B-Q. The chicken shack pours it over the bird and the white bread underneath, and the bread does the soaking.

*Tradition holds —* every shop guards its own mix, and the argument over whose is best runs shop by shop rather than recipe by recipe.

The trademark history runs through the sauce next door. Argia B. Collins Sr. was using the Mumbo name for a Chicago barbecue sauce from at least 1950; the Trademark Trial and Appeal Board later held that a D.C. company could not take that name from its Chicago founder. *Inference —* mild sauce and mumbo sauce are the same family of Black Chicago carryout condiment, one of which travelled east and picked up a second spelling.
text.how: Poured over the chicken in the box, not served beside it. A shop with a squeeze bottle asks whether you want mild sauce, hot sauce, both, or neither; both means the mild goes on first. The bread at the bottom of the box is part of the delivery system.
text.today: Sold bottled by several small makers and mixed in-house at the shacks. As of 16 September 2026 the USDA label panel for Aisha's Mild Sauce reads 280 mg sodium and 11 g sugar in a 2-tablespoon serving — 140 mg and 5.5 g in one tablespoon. No maker publishes a Scoville figure, and the shacks' own sauces carry no label.

kin.as: The style built around it: a shack, a fryer, white bread and this poured over.
Its D.C. cousin, and the one that carries the registered Chicago trademark.
One of the shops that made it popular, and where the pour goes over bread.

The bread at the bottom of the box is what catches it.
Why 'mild' here names a sauce rather than a heat level.
The supermarket relative: same sweet tomato family, different city and a corn-syrup lead.

confusable_with.tell: The word. Both are sweet tomato carryout sauces; Chicago says mild sauce, D.C. says mumbo or mambo.
