ingredients: half a dozen teaspoonfuls, each, of powdered allspice, cloves and cinnamon
recipes.text: Peel, and cut up together three dozen large tomatoes and a dozen onions. Chop into bits half a dozen green peppers and mix with the tomatoes and onions. Stir together a teacupful of brown sugar, five tablespoonfuls of salt, half a dozen teaspoonfuls, each, of powdered allspice, cloves and cinnamon, two teaspoonfuls of ground ginger, and a saltspoonful of paprika. Put these spices into three quarts of vinegar, add the vegetables, mix thoroughly, and cook steadily for two hours. When cold, bottle and seal.
recipes.note: Copied verbatim, old spellings kept. A pre-1930 American bottled tomato sauce, sweet and spiced and vinegared — the shelf ancestor of the ketchup-and-barbecue-sauce mixes the shacks make now, not a recipe for mild sauce itself.

names.name: Mumbo sauce
names.said: Ordered by the squeeze: 'wings and fries, mumbo on everything.' Spelled mumbo in Chicago and on the trademark, mambo on plenty of D.C. counters.

text.what: A carryout condiment of Washington, D.C.: red-orange, thick, poured over fried chicken wings, french fries, fried jumbo shrimp and fried rice. Close to barbecue sauce but sweeter, and either spicier or more sour depending on whose it is. The consistency and the flavour vary shop to shop. Its origin and its ingredients are both disputed, and so is its spelling.
text.story:
The trademark belongs to Chicago. Argia B. Collins Sr. used the Mumbo name for a barbecue sauce he developed for his Chicago restaurant from at least 1950; his successor-in-interest, Select Brands, LLC, registered it with the US Patent and Trademark Office on 25 May 1999, Registration No. 2,247,855. Select Brands has challenged D.C. sellers who use the term.

The D.C. account runs through a restaurant called Wings-n-Things in the late 1960s, according to Capital City Mumbo Sauce. A John Young's Wings-n-Things had been serving mumbo sauce on chicken wings in Buffalo, New York since the early 1960s, and Young credited a Washington, D.C. restaurant for the sauce — a boxer had told him a D.C. place was doing good business in wings, so he specialised. Since Collins's sauce runs back to the 1950s, before it showed up at Wings-n-Things, the D.C. version is speculated to be a transplant of the Chicago original. After two years of argument the Trademark Trial and Appeal Board found that a D.C.-based company could not take the name from its Chicago founder.

It stays a live argument in the city. In 2018 Mayor Muriel Bowser called mumbo sauce "annoying" in a Facebook post and questioned whether it was "quintessential" D.C.; her spokesperson said the remarks were meant to liven Thanksgiving discussions. McDonald's released a limited-time version on 9 October 2023 with a media campaign and a short YouTube documentary on the sauce's history.

The name carries beyond the counter: the go-go group Mambo Sauce took its name from it, Christylez Bacon performs a song about it, Black Flag Brewing in Columbia, Maryland named a beer Mambo Sauce, and Camille Acker's collection Training School for Negro Girls contains a story called "Mambo Sauce".
text.how: Poured, not tossed. A carryout squeezes it over the wings and the fries in the box so both arrive wet, or hands it over in a lidded cup. Every shop mixes its own; the bottled Capital City version starts with ketchup, then sugar, then water, then soy sauce, and takes its heat from a cayenne pepper hot sauce well down the list.
text.today: Bottled by Capital City and by others, and made in-house at carryouts across the District. As of 16 September 2026 the USDA label panel for Capital City Mild Mambo Sauce reads 160 mg sodium and 10 g sugar in a 2-tablespoon serving — 80 mg and 5 g in one tablespoon. Nobody publishes a Scoville number for it. The house sauces have no label at all.

recipes.title: Chili sauce (No. 2)
recipes.author: Marion Harland
ingredients: three teaspoonfuls, each, of powdered allspice, cloves and cinnamon
recipes.text: Peel and chop two dozen ripe tomatoes and six onions. Remove the seeds from two red peppers and chop the peppers fine; then stir them into the tomatoes and onions. Season all with a teacupful of granulated sugar, four tablespoonfuls of salt, three teaspoonfuls, each, of powdered allspice, cloves and cinnamon, and a teaspoonful of ground ginger. Pour over all two quarts of vinegar, and boil in a porcelain-lined kettle for two and a half hours. When cool, bottle and seal.
recipes.note: Copied verbatim, old spellings kept. Not mumbo sauce — an American home 'chili sauce', tomato and vinegar and sugar and red pepper, bottled and kept. It is the shelf-stable tomato condiment the carryout sauces were later built on top of.

names.name: Nashville hot paste
names.said: Ordered by rung: mild, medium, hot, extra hot, and a top rung each shop names for itself.

text.what: A cayenne paste, spooned onto fried chicken the moment it leaves the fryer. Fat carries it — lard or a ladle of the frying oil itself — which is why it soaks in rather than sitting on top, and why the bird turns deep red. Some shops add sugar, garlic or extra hot sauce. Some apply it before breading instead of after. Recipes are kept close.
text.story:
Spicy fried chicken has been served in Nashville's African-American communities for generations; anecdotal evidence puts the dish as early as the 1930s, though the current style of spice paste may only run back to the mid-1970s.

The origin generally accepted belongs to the family of André Prince Jeffries, who has run Prince's Hot Chicken Shack since 1980. Before that it belonged to her great-uncle, Thornton Prince III. Jeffries says the development was an accident: Thornton was a womaniser, and after a late Saturday night his girlfriend cooked him a fried chicken breakfast with extra pepper as revenge. He liked it. By the mid-1930s he and his brothers had their own recipe and had opened the BBQ Chicken Shack café.

By 2015 an estimated two dozen restaurants in the Nashville area served hot chicken. Bill Purcell, mayor of Nashville, sponsored the Music City Hot Chicken Festival and called his table at Prince's his "second office". KFC began selling Nashville Hot Chicken across its US restaurants in January 2016 after a Pittsburgh-area trial it called the most successful product testing in its recent history, and ran it in the UK from 22 May to 18 June 2017. Buffalo Wild Wings offers Nashville hot-style wings.

*Inference —* the paste is the only sauce in this set that is applied with a spoon and a gloved hand rather than poured or shaken, and that is what keeps it off supermarket shelves in its own form.
text.how: Fry the wings. While they drain, whisk cayenne and the shop's other powders into hot fat — lard, or oil dipped straight out of the fryer. Spoon it over with a gloved hand and squeeze it lightly into the crust. White bread underneath catches what runs off; pickle chips go on top. Sauce and bird are never separated, so there is no dip and no bowl.
text.today: Sold across Nashville and, since 2016, by chains that bottle or powder an approximation. Frank's RedHot sells a Nashville Hot Wings Sauce whose label reads 340 mg sodium and 2 g sugar in a tablespoon as of 16 September 2026 — vinegar-led, with canola oil fourth, which is a bottle's answer to a paste. The shacks' own pastes have no label, no sodium figure and no Scoville number, and are held as secrets.

names.name: Old Bay Seasoning
names.said: In Baltimore it goes on the wings without being ordered, the way blue cheese arrives in Buffalo.

text.what: A blend of eighteen herbs and spices built on celery salt — salt and celery seed — with red pepper, black pepper and paprika. Bay leaves, mustard, cardamom, cloves and ginger are among the others listed for the original product held at the Baltimore Museum of Industry. Made for crab and shrimp; used on wings, fries, popcorn, eggs, corn and a great deal else across Maryland, Virginia and the rest of the Mid-Atlantic.
text.story:
Gustav Brunn built a wholesale spice business in Wertheim, Germany, selling to food industries when spices ran short in the hyperinflation after the First World War. The company moved to Frankfurt after the Nazi Party took power. Kristallnacht led to Brunn's arrest and his being sent to Buchenwald. According to his son, Brunn's wife paid a lawyer a large sum to get him released; the family already held American visas, and they escaped to New York City and then to Baltimore, where Brunn had relatives.

He arrived with a small spice grinder. In 1939 he founded the Baltimore Spice Company and produced "Delicious Brand Shrimp and Crab Seasoning", later renamed Old Bay after the Baltimore Steam Packet Company — the "Old Bay Line" — which ran passenger ships from Baltimore to Norfolk in the early 1900s.

McCormick & Company of Hunt Valley, Maryland bought the brand in 1990 and kept the yellow can. In 2017 McCormick switched Old Bay to plastic containers to cut packaging costs; in December 2025 it announced a return to metal cans.

The seasoning kept colonising things. Utz made a Crab Chip on a similar blend; Herr's uses Old Bay itself; Lay's brought out Chesapeake Bay Crab Spice chips in 2018. Baltimore bars sell a 'Crabby Bo' — a National Bohemian beer whose glass rim is wetted and dipped in the seasoning. Flying Dog brewed Dead Rise for the 75th anniversary in 2014, and George's Beverage Company made Old Bay vodka in 2022. McCormick launched Old Bay Hot Sauce ahead of Super Bowl LIV in 2020; the 10 fl oz bottles retailed at $3.49, sold out in thirty minutes, crashed the website, and resold online for between $50 and $200.
text.how: Shaken over the wings hot out of the fryer, dry, with nothing wet underneath — the celery salt does the work a sauce would. Some Baltimore kitchens go wet: melted butter first, then the shake, which turns it into a paste that clings. Also goes on the fries in the same basket.
text.today: Made by McCormick, sold in the yellow can again from December 2025. As of 16 September 2026 the USDA label panel recorded for the seasoning reads 140 mg sodium in a ¼-teaspoon serving; that works out to 1,680 mg in a tablespoon, a figure the arithmetic gives and nobody eats. The label declares no sugar line. There is no Scoville number for it and there never has been.

names.name: Ranch dressing
names.said: Say 'ranch' anywhere in America and a cup arrives. Say it in Buffalo and somebody looks up.

text.what: A savoury creamy dressing of buttermilk, salt, garlic, onion, black pepper and herbs — commonly chives, parsley and dill — mixed into mayonnaise or another oil emulsion. Sour cream and yogurt sometimes stand in for the buttermilk or the mayonnaise. It has been the best-selling salad dressing in the United States since 1992, when it passed Italian, and it is the most popular wing dip in the country.
text.story:
Steve Henson made the first version in the early 1950s in the Anchorage area, where he worked as a plumbing contractor and cooked for his crews. He retired from plumbing at thirty-five, moved with his wife Gayle to Santa Barbara County, California, and in 1956 bought a guest ranch in San Marcos Pass which he renamed Hidden Valley Ranch. He served the dressing at the ranch steakhouse; guests bought jars to take home. His friend Audrey Ovington, owner of Cold Spring Tavern, was the first commercial customer. By 1957 he was selling packets of mix in stores, and mail-ordering the dry ingredients at 75 cents apiece until every room in the house was given over to it.

The Hensons incorporated, built a factory, and sold nationally. Manufacturing moved to San Jose, then Colorado, then Sparks, Nevada in 1972. In October 1972 Clorox bought Hidden Valley Ranch for $8 million and Henson retired. Clorox reformulated it several times — adding buttermilk flavouring to the seasoning so the dressing could be made with cheaper regular milk — and in 1983 developed a shelf-stable bottled version.

The name started a fight. Ranch Style Beans had been on sale since the early 1930s, and in 1975 its Texas maker Waples-Platter sued Kraft Foods and General Foods for using "ranch style" on salad dressings. Judge Eldon Brooks Mahon tried the case in Fort Worth in 1976 and ruled for Waples-Platter; his opinion catalogues the ranch and ranch-style products then on the market, most of them built to compete with Hidden Valley. Henson himself was deposed about the history.

It reached the wing through pizza. Domino's began offering ranch as a condiment with its chicken wings and pizzas in 1994, and the pairing took. Cool Ranch Doritos had arrived in 1987; Hidden Valley Ranch Wavy Lay's in 1994.
text.how: Cold, in a cup, beside the wing. Home versions mix buttermilk, mayonnaise and sour cream with lemon juice, minced garlic, onion powder, black pepper and dried herbs, and want an hour in the refrigerator before the herbs give anything up. It doubles as the dip for the celery and carrots and as the dressing on the salad nobody ordered.
text.today: Best-selling dressing in the country and, by the count in the standard wing description, the most popular wing dip. In 2017 a study by the Association for Dressings and Sauces found 40% of Americans named ranch their favourite dressing. As of 16 September 2026 the USDA label panel for Hidden Valley Original Ranch Topping & Dip reads 240 mg sodium and 1 g sugar in a 2-tablespoon serving — 120 mg and 0.5 g in one tablespoon. Soybean oil first, egg yolk third, buttermilk sixth. No Scoville number, and nothing on the label to warrant one.

names.name: Soy garlic sauce
names.said: Ganjang (간장) is soy sauce. A Korean counter offers soy garlic or spicy, and banban gets you both.

text.what: A brown glaze of soy sauce, sugar and garlic, brushed onto fried chicken after the fryer. Sweet and savoury rather than hot; often heavily garlicky. Ganjang-chikin — soy sauce chicken — is the Korean name for the dish it makes. A honey version, sweeter and stickier, is sold alongside it.
text.story:
Bonchon standardised two flagship sauces, soy garlic and spicy, made with regional Korean ingredients and manufactured centrally in South Korean facilities so every franchise tastes the same. Jinduk Seo founded the chain in Busan in 2002; its name means "my hometown". Its first US location was in Fort Lee, New Jersey, and it is credited as the first Korean fried chicken brand to expand internationally.

The sauce sits in an old lineage. Pogye (포계), a fried chicken dish of the early Joseon dynasty, was sautéed in oil while soy sauce, sesame oil, flour-and-water and vinegar were poured on in turn.

Bonchon stopped retailing in South Korea by the end of 2016 to concentrate on export. VIG Partners took a majority stake in December 2018; the headquarters moved to Dallas, Texas in 2021. Around 500 restaurants operate in over ten countries.

*Inference —* soy garlic is the sauce that carried Korean fried chicken to people who do not want heat, which is most of a mall food court.
text.how: Double-fry, then paint. The sugar in the glaze catches on a still-hot crust and sets glossy; too much of it and the crust goes soft, which is why it is brushed thin rather than tossed. Serve with pickled radish. Scallion-topped padak is the same bird under shredded scallion instead.
text.today: Sold at Korean fried chicken chains across the United States and bottled by small importers. As of 16 September 2026 the USDA label panel for We Love You Soy Garlic Korean Chicken Wing Sauce & Glaze reads 430 mg sodium and 6 g sugar in a 1-tablespoon serving, with soy sauce first, sugar second and granulated garlic fourth. Black pepper is the only pepper on it, and no Scoville number is published — for a sauce that claims no heat, none is expected.

names.name: Sweet chili sauce
aliases: น้ำจิ้มไก่
names.said: Nam chim kai (น้ำจิ้มไก่) is Thai for dipping sauce for chicken. The name says what it is for.

text.what: A clear, thickened red sauce of chillies, rice wine vinegar and sugar, often with garlic and sometimes fish sauce. Red chilli peppers — Fresno, Thai or red jalapeños — give it its flecks. Known in Thailand as nam chim kai, a dipping sauce for chicken, and used across Thai, Afghan, Malaysian and Western cooking. In European Chinese restaurants it is the dip for prawn toast, egg rolls, lettuce wraps, spring rolls and chicken wings.
text.story:
It arrived on American wing boards through the takeaway counter rather than the wing bar. In Australia, New Zealand, Europe, Canada and the United States it is stocked as a condiment in takeaway shops and supermarkets, and it is sold bottled everywhere.

The wing board made room for it. As the wing market grew, restaurants created and used sauces beyond Buffalo, some of them drawn from Chinese, Japanese, Thai, Caribbean and Indian cooking.

*Inference —* sweet chili is the sauce that taught American wing menus that sweet and chile could sit in the same bottle without tomato between them. Hot honey and mango habanero both work the same seam.
text.how: Straight from the bottle. It is already thickened, so it coats a fried wing without warming and does not need butter or oil to carry it. Toss, or serve in a cup as a dip. A kitchen after more heat adds sriracha or fresh chilli, and a kitchen after more bite adds lime.
text.today: On supermarket shelves and takeaway counters across the country, and on wing boards as a standing flavour. As of 16 September 2026 the USDA label panel for Ka-Me Sweet Chili Sauce reads 220 mg sodium and 6 g sugar in a 1-tablespoon serving, with water first, cane sugar second and pickled chili third. No Scoville number is published — usual for this shelf.

names.name: Teriyaki sauce
names.said: Teri (照り) is the shine the sugar gives; yaki (焼き) is grilling or broiling. The sauce is named for what it looks like after the heat.

text.what: Soy sauce, mirin or sake, and sugar, boiled down to a glaze. The Japanese name for it is tare (タレ). Traditionally the meat is dipped in it or brushed with it while cooking; ginger goes in sometimes, spring onion over the top. In North America the word covers any dish made with a teriyaki-like sauce, including versions using substitutes for sake or mirin, or adding sesame or garlic — both uncommon in Japanese cooking. It goes on chicken wings and is used as a dipping sauce.
text.story:
Teriyaki emerged as a cooking technique in Japan during the Edo period; it is believed to have developed during the 1600s. Fish carry it there — yellowtail, marlin, skipjack tuna, salmon, trout, mackerel — while the West puts it on chicken, pork, lamb and beef.

Japanese immigrants brought it to Hawaii, where it changed with local ingredients and became a fixture of the plate lunch. Seattle grew a teriyaki culture of its own in the 1990s; by 2010 more than eighty-three restaurants in the city had teriyaki in the name, and some outlets call it the city's signature cuisine. The first standalone teriyaki restaurant, Toshi's Teriyaki, opened in Lower Queen Anne in 1976, selling low-cost chicken and beef skewers; by 1996 it had grown to seventeen locations.

The American sauce is generally sweet, though it can be made spicy. Pineapple juice is sometimes used — it sweetens and its bromelain enzymes tenderise the meat. Grilling first and pouring the sauce on afterwards, or using sweet sauce as a marinade, are both non-traditional methods.

*Inference —* the teriyaki wing came off the plate lunch and the skewer counter, not off a Buffalo menu, and arrived on wing boards already familiar to everyone.
text.how: Blend soy sauce, sake or mirin and sugar over heat, boil and reduce to the thickness you want. Brush it on the wings while they grill or broil, in coats, letting each set before the next. For fried wings, toss them in the reduced sauce off the heat. Cornstarch, potato starch or kuzu root starch thickens a thin one. Sugar is why it goes on late: it darkens fast over direct heat.
text.today: Bottled by every large soy-sauce maker and on wing boards nationally. As of 16 September 2026 the USDA label panel for Kikkoman Teriyaki Marinade & Sauce reads 610 mg sodium and 2 g sugar in a 1-tablespoon serving — the highest sodium per tablespoon of any sauce measured for this set, ahead of Frank's RedHot at 570. Soy sauce is first; no chile appears on the label and no Scoville number is published.

names.name: Yangnyeom sauce
names.said: 양념 means seasoning. Order banban — 반반, half-half — and the box arrives half in this sauce, half plain.

text.what: A sweet and spicy glaze built on gochujang — a fermented Korean paste of red chili powder, glutinous rice, fermented soybean powder, barley malt powder and salt — with garlic, sugar and other seasonings. Painted onto fried chicken with a brush after the fryer, in a thin even coat rather than a toss. Yangnyeom chicken is the dish; this is what makes it.
text.story:
Yun Jonggye started it in 1982, at a fried chicken restaurant in Daegu that later became Mexican Chicken. He noticed customers struggling with the hard, crisp layers of fried chicken — scraped palates among the complaints — and decided to soften the shell by marinating the bird sweet and spicy.

The ground was already laid. Frying chicken in Korea goes back centuries; pogye (포계) in the early Joseon dynasty was sautéed in oil with soy sauce, sesame oil, flour-and-water and vinegar poured on in turn. Chicken-eating took off in the late 1960s when Myeongdong Yeongyang Center began selling whole chicken roasted over an electric oven, and US military presence after the Korean War brought deep-frying. The first modern franchise, Lims Chicken, opened in 1977 in the basement of the Shinsegae Department Store on Chungmu-ro in Seoul. Beer made it a habit: chimaek, from chicken and maekju.

Gochujang itself is older than the chile in it. Pepper paste appears in Korean texts from 1433 and 1445, before chili peppers reached Korea — Portuguese traders brought those to East Asia in the early 16th century. Sunchang gochujang has been a regional speciality since the 14th century.

Julia Moskin of The New York Times called yangnyeom chicken "the apotheosis of the Korean style" of fried chicken. By 2026 there were 40,000 fried chicken restaurants in South Korea and 1,800 more run internationally by Korean brands in sixty countries.
text.how: Double-fry first, so the crust can take a wet coat without going soft. Warm the sauce, then hand-paint it on with a brush — the point is a thin layer over the whole bird rather than a soaked one. Serve with pickled radish and beer. Half-and-half orders get one sauce and one plain in the same box.
text.today: Made in-house at Korean fried chicken shops and sold bottled by several importers. As of 16 September 2026 the USDA label panel for Roland Spicy Gochujang Korean BBQ Sauce reads 469 mg sodium and 7 g sugar in a 2-tablespoon serving — 234 mg and 3.5 g in one tablespoon, with red pepper paste second. Nobody publishes a Scoville number. Gochujang has its own scale, the Gochujang hot-taste unit, measured by chromatography of capsaicin and dihydrocapsaicin and sorted into five levels from Mild to Extreme Hot — but that rates the paste, not a finished sauce.

kin.as: The style is this glaze, the double fry and the box it arrives in.
The other half of the order, and the sauce most shops pair it against.
The crust that lets a wet glaze go on without collapsing.

names.name: beef on weck
names.said: Weck rhymes with deck. Order it rare, dipped, with horseradish, and expect to be asked how much.

text.what: Rare roast beef, hand-carved thin, on a kummelweck roll topped with kosher salt and caraway seeds. The cut face of the top half gets dipped in jus from the roast; prepared horseradish comes on the side for the eater to spread. Along with wings and sponge candy it is one of the three best-known Buffalo specialties.
text.story:
The sandwich predates the wing by roughly a century, though its history is not well established. A German baker named William Wahr, thought to have come from the Black Forest, is believed to have made the kummelweck roll in Buffalo, possibly modelled on the Swabian Schwäbische Seele, a thin salt-and-caraway roll left as a ceremonial offering for the dead. A Western New York butcher puts the sandwich's creation somewhere in the mid-19th century. A local pub owner is said to have built it on the salted roll so the salt would sell more drink.

Kümmel is German for caraway and Weck means roll in the south-western dialects of the Palatinate, the Saarland, Baden and Swabia. The American roll ended up softer and fluffier than a German Kümmelbrötchen. Buffalo-area bakeries are the only commercial source for it.

The wing dragged the sandwich out of town. Buffalo Wild Wings was started by former Western New York residents and opened as "Buffalo Wild Wings and Weck", abbreviated BW3 — the third W was the weck. The chain dropped it in 1998 and some people still say BW3.
text.how: Roast the beef slowly, keep it rare, and carve it thin by hand, often at a carving station in view. Dip the cut face of the top half of the roll in the jus. Leave the horseradish to the eater. The salt on the crust is coarse and it is meant to be tasted, which is the part a bar counted on.
text.today: Expatriates carried it: PJ's BAR-B-QSA in Saratoga Springs is noted for its version, and Bobby Flay and Anthony Bourdain have both put it on television. *Inference —* the roll is the limit on how far it travels, because nobody outside Buffalo bakes it commercially.

names.name: boneless wings
names.said: Ordered by count like a wing and priced like a wing. A kitchen that sells both will ask bone-in or boneless before it asks the sauce.

text.what: Small pieces of skinless, boneless chicken breast coated in flour and spices, then fried or baked, like a chicken nugget, and tossed in or served with the same sauces as a Buffalo wing. Restaurants began offering them after the price of raw wings rose and as some diners wanted a neater way to eat; they are sometimes marketed under the name wyngz.
text.story:
The argument over the word reached a state supreme court. On 25 July 2024 the Supreme Court of Ohio decided Berkheimer v. REKM, L.L.C., slip op. No. 2024-Ohio-2787, 4 to 3. Michael Berkheimer had ordered boneless wings with parmesan garlic sauce at Wings on Brookwood in Hamilton, Ohio, in 2016. A bone lodged in his esophagus and tore it, and the tear caused an infection; CBS News reports the bone at 5 centimetres, while a law-firm note on the case describes it as roughly 1 3/8 inches. He sued, saying the restaurant failed to warn him that boneless wings could contain bones. The trial court gave the restaurant summary judgment and the appeals court affirmed.

Justice Joseph T. Deters wrote for the majority. The Associated Press reports the opinion holding that a diner reading boneless wings on a menu would no more believe the restaurant was warranting the absence of bones than a person eating chicken fingers would think he had been served fingers. CBS News quotes the opinion directly: "The food item's label on the menu described a cooking style; it was not a guarantee."

Justice Michael P. Donnelly dissented, joined by Justices Melody J. Stewart and Jennifer Brunner. He called the majority's reasoning "utter jabberwocky". Of the word itself he wrote: "When they read the word 'boneless,' they think that it means 'without bones,' as do all sensible people." And of the jury the case never reached: "Does anyone really believe that the parents in this country who feed their young children boneless wings or chicken tenders or chicken nuggets or chicken fingers expect bones to be in the chicken? Of course they don't".

*Inference —* the two opinions are arguing about different things. One asks what a menu word does — names a preparation — and the other asks what a customer hears. This project records both and adjudicates neither; the court's own count was four to three.
text.how: Cut breast into roughly one-inch pieces. Dredge in seasoned flour, or batter, then fry or bake. Sauce goes on the same way it goes on a wing: into a bowl, sauce poured over, shaken. Because there is no skin and no bone, the coating is doing all the work the skin does on a bone-in wing, and it goes soft faster once the sauce hits it.
text.today: On the menu at nearly every chain and most bars, usually priced per piece against the bone-in count on the same board. *Inference —* the price gap moves with the wholesale wing market rather than with the cost of breast meat, which is why the boneless order is sometimes the cheaper one and sometimes not.

names.name: buffalo chicken dip
names.said: Brought in the dish it was baked in, set on a towel, eaten with whatever is nearest.

text.what: Shredded chicken, cream cheese, cayenne-and-butter wing sauce and a dairy dressing, baked until it bubbles and eaten hot with chips, celery or bread. It takes the flavour of a wing and removes the bone, the skin, the fryer and the plate.
text.story:
The dish belongs to a wider pattern the wing set off. Buffalo as a name is now applied to other spiced fried foods served with dipping sauces — boneless wings, chicken fries, chicken nuggets, popcorn chicken, shrimp, cauliflower — and to dishes seasoned with the sauce rather than fried at all, pizza among them. The sauce travelled and the method stayed behind.

The occasion carried it. The Super Bowl is the second-largest event for American food consumption, behind Thanksgiving dinner, and a baked dip suits a room where nobody is running a fryer.

*Tradition holds —* the dip is a 1990s-and-after home invention, spread by recipe cards, community cookbooks and hot-sauce marketing rather than by any restaurant. This project has not found a source that names a first cook or a first year, and the origin is recorded here as unsettled rather than as anyone's.
text.how: Shred cooked chicken. Beat it into softened cream cheese with cayenne pepper sauce and butter, or with bottled wing sauce, then fold in blue cheese or ranch dressing and shredded cheese. Bake until it bubbles at the edge. Serve hot in the baking dish with celery, carrots, tortilla chips or torn bread. Cold, it sets solid and is reheated rather than eaten.
text.today: A fixture of American party tables in winter, and a standing item in supermarket deli cases around the Super Bowl. *Inference —* the dip is how the Buffalo flavour reaches households that will not deep-fry indoors, which is most of them.

text.what: A pizza sauced with cayenne-and-butter wing sauce instead of tomato, topped with chicken and mozzarella, and finished with blue cheese or ranch. Buffalo is applied here to a dish that is seasoned with the sauce rather than fried in the style at all.
text.story:
The pizza chains and the wing arrived at each other from both directions. In 1994, following four Super Bowl appearances by the Buffalo Bills, Domino's added Buffalo wings to its national menu, and Pizza Hut followed the next year. The wing went onto the pizza menu first; the sauce went onto the pizza after.

*Inference —* the order runs the other way in Buffalo itself, where pizzerias were already selling wings out of the same kitchen. A shop with a fryer for wings and an oven for pizza has both halves of this dish on the line before anyone names it.
text.how: Brush the base with wing sauce in place of tomato. Cooked chicken — often the same breast meat a boneless order uses — mozzarella, sometimes red onion. Bake. Finish with a drizzle of blue cheese or ranch after the oven, not before, so the dressing does not split. Celery on the side is optional and in Buffalo it is not.
text.today: Carried by national chains and by independent pizzerias in Western New York, where the wing and the pie have shared a counter for decades. *Inference —* the dish is the clearest case of Buffalo as a flavour word: nothing about it is fried, and the name still reads.

names.name: celery and carrots
names.said: Nobody orders it. It arrives. In Buffalo a medium order comes with celery and blue cheese whether you asked or not.

text.what: Cut celery, usually with carrot sticks, served cold beside hot wings with a cup of blue cheese or ranch that both the vegetables and the wings go into. Celery here is the petiole — the leaf stalk of Apium graveolens — cut raw to finger length. It cools the mouth between wings, it carries dip, and it is the one item on the plate nobody asks for.
text.story:
The Anchor Bar's account puts the vegetables on the plate from the first night: on 4 March 1964 Teressa Bellissimo fried wings for her son Dominic's friends and brought out cut celery and blue cheese for dipping as hors d'oeuvres. The celery was there to be grabbed because celery was everywhere. The New York Public Library's historical menu archive shows it as the third-most-popular item on New York City menus through the 19th and early 20th centuries, behind only coffee and tea, served in celery vases to be salted and eaten raw; whole varieties have since vanished because they were hard to grow and did not ship. North American commercial growing narrowed onto one cultivar, 'Pascal'.

*Inference —* the wing plate kept a garnish the rest of American dining dropped, so a bar basket in 2026 preserves a habit the city around it stopped having.
text.how: Cut the petiole into sticks a little longer than a wing. The strings that peel off a stalk are bundles of angular collenchyma cells sitting outside the vascular bundles, which is why celery pulls apart lengthways and not across. Carrots go in raw, as sticks or as whole small carrots. Everything serves cold against hot wings, with the dip in its own cup. Freshly cut celery decays fast, so a kitchen cuts near service and keeps it at 0–2 °C.
text.today: Wingstop sells veggie sticks — carrots and/or celery — as a side you pay for. A Buffalo counter still puts them on the plate unasked. *Tradition holds —* the celery is the first thing left in the basket and the last thing a Buffalo bar would stop putting there.

names.name: chicken and waffles
names.said: Butter and syrup on the waffle, hot sauce on the chicken, and the two meet in the middle of the plate.

text.what: Fried chicken on a waffle, eaten with butter and syrup as a waffle would be, and often with hot sauce. It belongs to several culinary traditions at once — Pennsylvania Dutch cuisine and soul food among them — and the two versions are not the same dish.
text.story:
The Pennsylvania Dutch version came first and is not fried: pulled, stewed chicken over a plain waffle, covered in gravy, appearing in the 1600s in Pennsylvania Dutch country. Waffles entered American cuisine with European colonists in the 1600s, and the food's popularity rose after 1789 when Thomas Jefferson bought four waffle irons in Amsterdam. In the early 1800s hotels and resorts outside Philadelphia served waffles with fried catfish; fried chicken gradually replaced the catfish because catfish was seasonal. By the 1860s waffles with chicken and gravy were a common Sunday dish among the Pennsylvania Dutch. By the 1840s broiled chicken and waffles were the celebrated specialty at Warriner's Tavern in Springfield, Massachusetts, run by Jeremy and Phoebe Warriner, two well-known abolitionists.

The fried version is associated with the American South and with soul food, and it grew after the Wells Supper Club opened in Harlem in 1938; the dish was served in Harlem as early as the 1930s at Tillie's Chicken Shack and Richard Wells's jazz nightclub, and in 1935 the trumpeter Bunny Berigan composed an instrumental called "Chicken and Waffles". A traditional account within soul food holds that the combination was a delicacy, and it remained "a special-occasion meal in African American families" for decades. The combination is absent from early Southern cookbooks — not in Mrs. Porter's Southern Cookery Book of 1871, nor in Abby Fisher's What Mrs. Fisher Knows About Old Southern Cooking of 1881, generally considered the first cookbook written by an African American — which may point to a later origin than the traditional account suggests.

Los Angeles got it by 1931, at a restaurant called The Maryland which marketed it as a Southern specialty, and again from 1975 onward through Herb Hudson's Roscoe's House of Chicken and Waffles, opened by a former Harlem resident and now a small chain.
text.how: Fry the chicken — bone-in pieces, or wings on a wing menu. Bake the waffle to order and serve it as a breakfast waffle, with butter and syrup. Chicken goes on top or beside. Hot sauce is the eater's call; in Baltimore, where the dish is popular enough to be a local custom, so is the order in which it goes on.
text.today: Served in specialty restaurants across the United States and on brunch menus that have never heard of Harlem or Lancaster County. *Inference —* the wing version is the newest branch: a wing menu can do the whole dish without a second fryer setting, and it lets a bar sell breakfast at eleven at night.

text.what: An Italian-American pasta dish from the Utica–Rome area of New York: chicken, rigatoni, and hot or sweet peppers in a spicy cream-and-tomato sauce. Variations are many; the peppers and the rigatoni are the constants.
text.story:
Its origin is unclear, and many chefs from the Utica area claim the dish.

*Inference —* that sentence is the same sentence upstate New York keeps writing about its own food. A hundred miles west, three Bellissimo accounts and one John Young compete over a wing; here a dozen Utica kitchens compete over a pasta, and in neither case does a document settle it. What both traditions do instead is hold contests.
text.how: Brown chicken, build a sauce of tomato and cream, and load it with peppers — cherry peppers for heat, sweet peppers for the other way. Toss through rigatoni, whose ridges and bore hold a sauce that thin-walled pasta would shed.
text.today: Served across the Utica–Rome corridor as a restaurant staple and a home dish. *Tradition holds —* riggies, greens and half-moons are the three things a Utica table names as its own.

names.name: french fries
names.said: An order is a side until somebody dumps the wings on top of it, and then it is the plate.

text.what: Potatoes cut into even batonnet or julienne strips, dried, and deep-fried. Beside wings they do three jobs: they soak the sauce that drips, they stretch a small order into a meal, and in several cities they become the plate the wings sit on.
text.story:
The fry arrived at the wing counter already carrying its own argument about fat. Beef suet was recommended as the superior frying medium in the older literature, and Belgian practice calls for filtered cattle fat — blanc de boeuf, ossewit. McDonald's fried in a mixture of 93% beef tallow and 7% cottonseed oil until 1990, when it changed to vegetable oil with beef flavouring. Horse fat was standard in northern France and Belgium until recently.

*Inference —* that switch is the same argument a wing shop has with itself, one fryer down: the fat is the flavour, and the fat is also the thing a chain answers to a nutrition panel for.
text.how: Cut even strips and dry them. Fry twice: a first bath at about 160 °C / 320 °F to cook the potato through, then a second at about 190 °C / 375 °F to crisp the outside. For thin 2–3 mm strips the first bath runs about three minutes and the second only seconds. Salt out of the oil. Beside wings the fries usually come out of the same oil as the wings, which means they taste of whatever else that fryer has been doing.
text.today: Wingstop lists fries among its sides alongside fried corn and veggie sticks. In Washington, D.C. the fries take mumbo sauce; in Chicago they go under the chicken and take mild sauce; in Atlanta they turn up as loaded fries under lemon pepper. *Inference —* wherever a city has its own wing sauce, it also has a fry that carries it.

names.name: the fried rice plate
names.said: Order across a turntable in bulletproof glass: wings over fried rice, mumbo on the side or on top.

text.what: Whole fried chicken wings served over egg fried rice with mumbo sauce, sold from Chinese-American carryouts across the Washington, D.C. metropolitan region. The wings are not cut; they go into the oil whole and come out as a set of three-jointed pieces laid over the rice.
text.story:
The dish belongs to two kitchens at once. Chinese-American restaurants pioneered take-out and delivery in the United States — New York delivery was pioneered in the 1970s by Empire Szechuan Gourmet Franchise, which hired Taiwanese students from Columbia to do it — and they were among the first American restaurants to use picture menus. Fried rice earned its place on those menus because it is fast, uses rice cooled overnight, and suited American tastes; the American version takes more soy sauce than the versions found in China.

Mumbo sauce came in from the other side of the counter. It is a takeout condiment specialty of Washington, D.C., put onto fried chicken wings, french fries, fried jumbo shrimp and fried rice, and it is often compared to Chicago's mild sauce, also a takeout sauce of that city's Black neighbourhoods.

*Inference —* the plate is what happens when a Chinese-American carryout menu meets a Black Washington sauce over the same counter, and neither side's cookbook explains it on its own.
text.how: Fry the wings whole and hard — no cut at the joints, so the drumette, flat and tip arrive attached. Bed of egg fried rice, made from rice cooled overnight. Sauce goes over the wings, or into a cup, depending on what the customer says. The whole thing comes in a hinged foam or plastic container and it is eaten with a plastic fork over the lid.
text.today: Still the standard order at Chinese-American carryouts across the DMV. *Tradition holds —* every regular has a position on whether the sauce goes over the rice or stays in the cup, and the counter asks.

names.name: Garbage Plate
names.said: Order it by what goes on it: two cheeseburgers, mac salad and home fries, hot sauce, onions, mustard. The name belongs to one restaurant; everyone else says plate.

text.what: Hot dog or hamburger meat and a meat hot sauce piled on a bed of side dishes — usually macaroni salad and home fries — with onions and mustard, and buttered bread alongside. Rochester's signature dish, and a trademark of one restaurant that every other restaurant has to work around.
text.story:
Alexander Tahou, a Greek immigrant, opened West Main Texas Hots in Rochester in 1918. The first version was hots — standard hot dogs or Rochester-style white hots — with potatoes, cold beans and buttered Italian bread. His son Nick took over in the 1940s, renamed the place Nick Tahou Hots, added hamburger meat and macaroni salad, and introduced the chili-like hot meat sauce that holds the dish together; that sauce came from a family recipe belonging to a Mexican friend of Alexander's.

The name arrived from outside. By the 1980s college students were coming in and asking for "that plate with all the garbage on it". The family resisted — as they put it, "it's food; it doesn't sound good" — then filed a United States trademark for Garbage Plate in 1991, which stopped anyone else selling one under that name. So Rochester eats trash plates, junkyard plates, hot plates, rubbish plates, sloppy plates and messy plates instead, and The Red Fern sells a vegan Compost Plate.

Jim Memmott of the Democrat and Chronicle called it "Rochester's signature thing", arguing it eclipses Kodak. In August 2017 the Rochester Red Wings briefly renamed themselves the Rochester Plates for the dish's centenary, brought the name back in 2018 for Thursday home games, and unveiled a plate-themed mascot named Mac in 2019.
text.how: Build from the bottom: two sides first — macaroni salad, home fries, french fries or beans — then the meat, then the hot meat sauce over everything, then raw onion and mustard. Buttered white bread on the side to push with. Eat it with a fork, standing or sitting, usually late.
text.today: Versions have spread past the Rochester metropolitan area to New York City, Pittsburgh, Raleigh and Denver. *Tradition holds —* the plate is widely eaten as a hangover remedy, and news outlets repeat that as often as they describe it.

names.name: jojo potatoes
names.said: Say jojo and a Portland counter knows what you mean; say potato wedge and you get something else.

text.what: A potato wedge that has been breaded, pressure-fried and spiced — not a bare wedge, and not a fry. The pressure fryer is a pressure cooker filled with hot oil, so the potato cooks fast and hard while keeping its water. Sold beside fried chicken across the Pacific Northwest, and in pockets of Montana, Minnesota, Nebraska, Northeast Ohio and upstate New York.
text.story:
Willamette Week ran down the origin in 2017 and found two accounts. Paul Nicewonger says his father, a Vancouver, Washington salesman, invented the jojo around 1958, demonstrating pressure fryers at a restaurant trade show next to Idaho potato vendors — he needed something cheap and quick to throw in the oil. Ron Echtenkamp of Ballantyne Strong credits Ed Nelson, a Flavor-Crisp salesman, with making them by accident at a Chicago trade show in 1961. The paper did not settle it.

The machine carried the food. Flavor-Crisp, Henny Penny and the Broaster Company of Beloit, Wisconsin built the pressure fryers, and "broasting" became the trade word for what came out of them. Because the fryers were sold region by region, each region came to believe it had invented the jojo.

*Inference —* the jojo is a salesman's demo that outlived the sales route, which is why its map looks like a distributor's territory rather than a cuisine.
text.how: Cut a potato into thick wedges with the skin on. Bread and season them, then pressure-fry. The lid holds steam over the oil, which raises the boiling point inside the fryer and cooks the wedge through before its crust burns. Out of the basket they go beside fried chicken, and in the same shops that sell chicken they take the same sauce the chicken takes.
text.today: Grocery-store delis and chicken counters across Oregon and Washington still sell them by the half-dozen. *Tradition holds —* a shop that calls them wedges is selling something else, and a shop that calls them jojos is usually running a pressure fryer.

names.name: mozzarella sticks
names.said: Ordered by the table, not the person, and judged on the pull.

text.what: Elongated pieces of mozzarella coated in breadcrumbs or batter and fried, served as an hors d'oeuvre with marinara. On a wing menu they are the thing a table orders when half of it does not want wings.
text.story:
Frying cheese in batter is old: a recipe for fried cheese sticks appears in Le Ménagier de Paris in 1393, though food historians hold that medieval French fried cheeses had little in common with what the modern stick became.

The American article dates to the 1970s. The historian Joel Jensen puts it down to two things arriving together: "the increasing availability of mass-produced mozzarella cheese beginning in the 1960s", and new efficient frying technologies for fast-paced food businesses such as bowling alleys and sports bars. The food writer Arthur Schwartz names mozzarella milanese — mozzarella dredged in flour, egg and breadcrumbs, then pan-fried — as the "prototype", a midweek Italian dish made from older mozzarella and eaten "within seconds" of leaving the pan.

*Inference —* the stick and the wing share a birth certificate. Both are cheap protein that only became a menu item once a bar had a fryer running all evening, and both spread through the same bowling alleys and sports bars in the same decade.
text.how: Cut mozzarella into fingers, coat in breadcrumbs or batter, and bake or fry in oil. Marinara for dipping is the restaurant default; plum sauce, jalapeño jelly, ketchup, barbecue sauce, honey mustard and ranch all appear. Serve immediately — the pull is the point and it is gone in minutes.
text.today: Provolone, Edam, cheddar and American are all fried the same way. In New York's Capital District the sticks come with raspberry sauce, which is regional and not a mistake. In American public schools, Bosco pizza sticks — soft breadsticks stuffed with mozzarella, with tomato sauce to dip — have become a staple.

names.name: mumbo fries
names.said: Fries, mumbo on top — or in the cup, which is a different order and the counter knows it.

text.what: French fries under mumbo sauce, from a Washington, D.C. carryout. Mumbo is a sweet, tangy, ketchup-based condiment — like barbecue sauce but sweeter, and somewhat spicier or more sour, with real variation in flavour and consistency between makers.
text.story:
The sauce arrives at the fries with a trademark fight attached. Argia B. Collins Sr. used the Mumbo name for a barbecue sauce he developed for his Chicago restaurant from at least as early as 1950; his successor-in-interest, Select Brands, LLC, registered the trademark on 25 May 1999, Registration No. 2,247,855, and has challenged D.C. uses of the name as infringements. Capital City Mumbo Sauce says the D.C. sauce started at a restaurant called Wings-n-Things in the late 1960s. John Young's Wings 'n Things had been serving mumbo sauce on chicken wings in Buffalo since the early 1960s, and Young himself credited a Washington, D.C. restaurant for the sauce. After two years of proceedings, the Trademark Trial and Appeal Board found that a D.C.-based company could not take the name from its Chicago founder.

In 2018 D.C. Mayor Muriel Bowser called mumbo sauce "annoying" in a Facebook post and questioned whether it was "quintessential" D.C.; her spokesperson said the remarks were meant to liven Thanksgiving discussions. On 9 October 2023 McDonald's released a version as a limited-time dipping sauce in its US locations, with a media campaign and a short YouTube documentary on the sauce's history.
text.how: Fry the potatoes, salt them, and ladle mumbo over the top so it soaks in at the edges and pools at the bottom of the container. A cup on the side instead is a live option and a live disagreement. The sauce is served at room temperature or warm, not hot.
text.today: Still a carryout order across the D.C. region, usually as the cheap half of a wing order. *Inference —* the fries are where a first-time customer meets the sauce, because they cost less than the wings and forgive a wrong guess about heat.

names.name: pickled radish
names.said: Comes in a small plastic tub, cubed, in its own liquid, and it is refilled without being asked.

text.what: Cubed pickled daikon in a sweet-sour brine, served cold in a small tub beside Korean fried chicken. Pickled radishes and beer or carbonated drinks are the standard accompaniment; Bonchon lists pickled radish among its side dishes alongside kimchi, coleslaw and Korean street corn.
text.story:
The pickle has a longer name than the tub suggests. Danmuji is the Korean name for takuan, the yellow daikon pickle credited to the Buddhist monk Takuan Sōhō (1573–1645). It came to Korea during the Japanese occupation and was first called dakkwang, a phonetic rendering of takuan; after the occupation ended it was renamed danmuji, meaning sweet radish pickle. The Korean version is usually sweeter and crunchier than the Japanese original.

*Tradition holds —* the cubed white version served with fried chicken is called chicken-mu, mu being the radish, and it is a distinct product from the long yellow danmuji sliced into kimbap. This project has not found a source that dates that split.

*Inference —* the tub does the job celery does in Buffalo and white bread does in Nashville: something cold, cheap and sharp arriving unasked against something hot and fatty. Three traditions, three answers, one problem.
text.how: Cut daikon into cubes and hold them in a sweetened vinegar brine until they go glassy and squeak. Serve cold, in liquid, in a lidded tub, with the chicken and the beer. Eat one between pieces.
text.today: Standard at Korean fried chicken shops in the United States, including chains that reached the US market after Korean brands expanded abroad. *Tradition holds —* the refill is free and the tub is the thing that runs out first.

text.what: Mozzarella, and often pepperoni, rolled in an egg-roll wrapper and deep-fried, served with marinara to dip. A Western New York bar snack that sits on the same appetizer list as wings and sells in freezer cases across upstate.
text.story:
The name is older than the Buffalo product. Barry Popik dates the phrase in print to 11 March 1970, in an advertisement in The Daily Herald of Provo, Utah for Jeno's Frozen Pizza Logs. The Buffalo article of the name belongs to Finger Food Products of Niagara Falls, New York, which claims a first use of "Original Pizza Logs" on 31 December 1992 and filed for the trademark on 7 February 2013; it registered on 8 October 2013.

*Inference —* the wrapper is the tell. Buffalo took an egg-roll skin off a Chinese-American supply shelf and put pizza inside it, which is the same move the city's Chinese-American carryouts made in the other direction with the wing.
text.how: Roll mozzarella, and pepperoni if it is going in, tight inside an egg-roll wrapper and seal the edge. Deep-fry until the wrapper blisters. Rest before serving or the cheese runs. Marinara in a cup; ranch in a cup if the table asks for it.
text.today: Sold frozen by the bag and hot by the basket across Western New York, and pushed as a stadium and arena snack — Popik records the Pittsburgh Penguins naming Pizza Logs their "Official Finger Food" in a post on 14 December 2018.

text.what: Draught beer sold by the jug for a table to share. It is the other half of a wing order almost everywhere wings are sold, and in two traditions it is named into the food: Hooters built its concept on wings and beer, and Korean has a single word for the pairing.
text.story:
Korean has the cleaner record of it. The first modern Korean fried chicken franchise, Lims Chicken, opened in 1977 in the basement of the Shinsegae Department Store on Chungmu-ro in Seoul, founded by Yu Seok-ho, and was "embraced as an excellent food pairing for draft beer". The word for that pairing, chimaek, is a portmanteau of chicken and maekju, the Korean word for beer. Pickled radishes and beer or carbonated drinks are the standard accompaniment to Korean fried chicken.

American bars said the same thing in marketing rather than in vocabulary. Hooters, founded in 1983, has put it plainly: "Customers can go to many places for wings and beer." Almost all Hooters restaurants hold licences to sell beer and wine. When a location closed, the company's own notice thanked its guests for "the many years of great times, cold beer, hot wings, and unforgettable memories shared here."

*Inference —* the pitcher is why the wing became bar food rather than restaurant food. Salt and heat sell drink, the drink carries the margin, and the wing was cheap enough in 1964 to be given away against it. Beef on weck is said to have worked the same trick in Buffalo a century earlier, with salt on a roll.
text.how: Pour from the pitcher into glasses at the table and keep pouring. Cold and light against salt, fat and cayenne; a dark or a high-alcohol beer fights the sauce rather than clearing it. Where a pitcher is not sold, the same job goes to a bucket of bottles, a soda refill, or in Korea to a shared bottle of lager.
text.today: Standard at American sports bars, and at Korean fried chicken shops that built the pairing into the language. *Tradition holds —* wing night and pitcher pricing move together, and a bar that drops one usually drops both.

names.said: The bread is under the chicken, not beside it, and by the end it is the best thing in the box.

text.what: Two slices of plain white sandwich bread with pickle chips on top, and the hot chicken laid over both. The bread catches the cayenne paste and the fat coming off the bird; the pickles cut it. It is not a side — it is the plate.
text.story:
Nashville hot chicken is served atop slices of white bread with pickle chips, and it is both the spice paste and that presentation that separate it from dishes like the Buffalo wing. The style comes out of African American communities in the Southern United States; anecdotal evidence puts spicy fried chicken in Nashville's Black neighbourhoods for generations, possibly from the 1930s, with the current style of paste dating only to the mid-1970s.

The originating family is generally accepted to be André Prince Jeffries's. She has run Prince's Hot Chicken Shack since 1980; before that it belonged to her great-uncle Thornton Prince III. Jeffries tells the development as an accident: after a late Saturday night, Thornton's girlfriend cooked him a fried chicken breakfast with extra pepper as revenge, and he liked it. By the mid-1930s he and his brothers had a recipe and the BBQ Chicken Shack.

*Inference —* the bread does the work celery does in Buffalo — something cheap and cold against something hot — but it does it underneath instead of alongside, and it ends up eaten rather than left.
text.how: Lay two slices flat in the box or on the paper. Pickle chips on the bread. Chicken straight out of the fryer on top, paste applied by the server with a spoon and gloves and pressed lightly into the crust by hand. Serve at once; the point is that the bread soaks.
text.today: Every Nashville hot chicken counter builds it this way, and the chains that took the style national — KFC's Nashville Hot from January 2016, and others — kept the paste and mostly dropped the bread. *Tradition holds —* eating the bread at the end is the standard finish, and the pickles are the only mercy on offer.

names.said: Six, ten, twenty, fifty. Say the number, then the heat, then the dip. The paper liner comes out soaked and that is the receipt.

text.what: The unit a bar sells wings in: a count of pieces in a basket or on a plate, lined with paper, with celery and carrots, a cup of blue cheese or ranch, and usually fries. A fry basket is the tool the wings come out of the oil in — it contains the food in the fryer and strains it on the way out — and the serving basket copies its shape.
text.story:
The count came from the knife. A wing off the bird is cut at both joints into a drumette, a flat and a tip; the tip is usually discarded or boiled for stock, so one wing sells as two pieces. Order twenty and twenty pieces arrive, which is roughly ten birds' worth of one wing each.

The basket came from the bar. Chains built around it — Buffalo Wild Wings from 1982, Hooters from 1983 — and Hooters put the pairing in its own words: "Customers can go to many places for wings and beer." Wingstop's sides sit where the wing shop's economics are clearest: fries, fried corn, and veggie sticks of carrots and/or celery, sold rather than given.

*Inference —* the basket is the reason a wing is counted instead of weighed, and the reason a shop can price heat, count and dip separately while charging for none of them by the pound.
text.how: Fry the pieces, drain them in the basket, tip them into a metal bowl, pour sauce over and shake. Into the lined basket, vegetables on top or beside, dip in a cup, fries underneath or alongside. Extra napkins, and wet wipes at counters that have learned. A dry-rub order skips the bowl and gets tossed with seasoning instead.
text.today: Standard at chains and independents alike. A shop that sells all flats or all drums charges for the privilege, because splitting a case by piece costs the kitchen its yield. *Tradition holds —* the number in a basket is the one thing about a wing order nobody argues over.

names.name: the air fryer
names.said: It is a small convection oven with a basket, and the word fryer in the name is doing a lot of work.

text.what: A small countertop convection oven that reaches deep-frying temperatures without submerging the food in oil. It circulates air at up to 200 °C / 392 °F to brown food coated in a thin layer of oil, where conventional frying drives the same browning reactions at 140–165 °C / 284–329 °F by putting the food in hot oil instead. Food sits in a basket over a drip tray, and for small pieces the basket must be shaken.
text.story:
The machine is younger than most people assume. Groupe SEB introduced the first air fryer in 2006 under the Actifry brand in the French market. The Dutch engineer Fred van der Weij invented it that same year and took it to Philips four years later; Philips launched the Airfryer at IFA Berlin in 2010 and patented the technique as Rapid Air. By 2018 air fryer was being used generically.

Adoption ran fast. A reported 36% of US households had a convection oven in 2020 and an estimated 60% in 2023; food manufacturers responded by adding air-frying instructions to products and selling pre-air-fried ones. In the UK a 2024 study claimed one in five Britons surveyed named the air fryer their most-used cooking device.

The verdict is not settled and this project does not settle it. Some reviewers find regular convection ovens or convection toaster ovens produce better results; others say air frying is essentially the same as convection baking; others praise the machines for cooking faster, being easier to clean and making crisp results easier than a full-size convection oven.

*Inference —* the wing is the machine's best case. It is small, it is mostly skin, and it carries its own fat, so the one thing the machine cannot supply is the one thing a wing brings with it.
text.how: Dry the wings, oil them thinly, and lay them in a single layer with space between; a crowded basket steams. Shake or turn partway, by hand or by the fryer's own paddle. Many cooks bring the baking powder trick over from the oven method. Sauce after, in a bowl, off the machine — sauce in the basket bakes onto the drip tray.
text.today: Sold as paddle types, cylindrical basket types up to about 2.8 litres, countertop convection ovens of about 24 litres with racks, halogen types under a radiant element, and barrel-shaped oil-less turkey fryers. *Tradition holds —* the tradition treats it as a home appliance rather than a shop one, and the shops that describe their method never describe this.

names.name: the baking powder bake
names.said: Baking powder, not baking soda. Recipe writers put that in capitals because readers keep getting it wrong.

text.what: The home method that gets wing skin to crisp in an oven: toss dried wings with baking powder and salt, bake low to render and dry, then hot to brown. No fryer, no pot of oil, and a crust that holds sauce for about as long as it takes to eat.
text.story:
The trick is a pH trick. Baking powder is alkaline — the opposite of acidic — so, as Christine Pittman of TheCookful puts it, "The addition of the baking powder therefore raises the pH level in the chicken, allowing the peptide bonds in the skin to break down, which in turn lets the skin get more crisp and brown." Nagi Maehashi of RecipeTin Eats describes the same result by a different mechanism: "the baking powder draws moisture to the surface of the skin so it can evaporate, thereby making the skin crispier."

The method arrived with the appliance. Convection — a fan moving air around the food to heat it evenly — was already in home ovens, and small countertop convection ovens are now marketed as air fryers; US household ownership was reported at 36% in 2020 and estimated at 60% in 2023.

*Inference —* this is the version of the wing most Americans actually cook. The fryer belongs to the bar; the oven belongs to the house, and the baking powder is what closes the gap between them.
text.how: Dry the wings thoroughly. Toss with baking powder and salt — RecipeTin Eats uses 5 teaspoons of baking powder and 3/4 teaspoon of salt for 4 lb / 2 kg of wings. Rack over a tray so air reaches underneath. Bake low first, 120 °C / 250 °F for 30 minutes, to render fat and dry the skin, then raise to 220 °C / 425 °F for 40–50 minutes to cook through and brown. Sauce after the oven. Use baking powder, not baking soda; RecipeTin Eats warns in capitals that readers who have swapped them found the result "INEDIBLE".
text.today: The standard home recipe across American food sites, and the method most often reached for on Super Bowl Sunday, the second-largest American eating day after Thanksgiving. *Inference —* the recipes agree on the ratio and the two temperatures and disagree on the chemistry, which suggests the method was found by cooking rather than by explanation.

names.name: the breaded fry
names.said: Rochester says breaded and means flour. Elsewhere breaded means crumbs, and the two do not eat alike.

text.what: Coating a wing before it goes in the oil — flour, seasoned flour, batter or crumbs — so the crust rather than the skin carries the crunch and holds the sauce. One common method for preparing food for deep frying involves adding multiple layers of batter around the food, such as cornmeal, flour or tempura; breadcrumbs may also be used.
text.story:
Breading was the Buffalo practice before bare frying was. From 1961 John Young served uncut chicken wings that were breaded, deep fried, and dressed in his own tomato-based mumbo sauce at John Young's Wings 'n Things; he had heard from a travelling boxer about a Washington, D.C. restaurant doing good business in wings and decided to specialise. He registered the name at the county courthouse and left the Buffalo area in 1970, and in 2013 the National Buffalo Wing Festival inducted him into its Hall of Flame.

The method did not leave the region when he did. It held seventy miles east, and it holds across fried chicken generally: Nashville's hot chicken is marinated in buttermilk, floured and fried before the paste goes on.

*Inference —* the coat changes what sauce does. On bare skin sauce sits and slides; on a crust it soaks, which is why breaded traditions tolerate a thinner, sweeter sauce than a bare fry does.
text.how: Dry the wing, then dredge — straight seasoned flour, or flour then egg then crumb for a thicker jacket. Rest the coated pieces a few minutes so the flour hydrates and stops shedding. Fry at 177–191 °C / 350–375 °F. A coated wing browns faster than a bare one, so it comes out earlier by eye, not by clock.
text.today: Standard across Rochester and through most of American fried chicken; the argument with Buffalo is seventy miles long and unresolved. *Tradition holds —* a shop that breads will describe its flour as a recipe, and a shop that fries bare will describe having no recipe at all.

names.name: the brine
names.said: Wet brine or dry. In a chicken kitchen the wet one is usually buttermilk and nobody calls it a brine.

text.what: Salting the bird before it cooks. Brining treats food with brine or coarse salt, which preserves and seasons it while enhancing tenderness. A wet brine immerses the meat in salt water; a dry brine covers it in coarse salt, which draws moisture out of the interior to the surface where it mixes with the salt and is then reabsorbed.
text.story:
Two accounts of the mechanism compete and both are current. In the first, salt ions enter the cells while other solutes stay trapped inside, raising cellular salinity so the cells take up water by osmosis and hold it through cooking. In the second, the salt denatures the cell's proteins, which coagulate into a matrix that traps water molecules and holds them during cooking. Meat and fish are typically brined for under 24 hours; heavy salting for preserving fish uses at least 20% salt, light salting for immediate eating 2–3%; a dry brine works over several hours.

Fried chicken traditions do it with dairy. Nearly all Nashville hot chicken is marinated in buttermilk, to impart flavour and to retain the meat's juices on frying.

*Inference —* on a wing the payoff is small and the risk is real. A wing is mostly skin and bone with little muscle to protect, so a long soak seasons the skin, softens it, and works against the crust the whole rest of the method is chasing. The dry version — salt, rack, fridge, overnight — is the one that suits the cut, and it is also what the baking powder method is quietly doing.
text.how: Wet: salt water, cold, under 24 hours, then dry the pieces thoroughly before any flour or any oil goes near them. Buttermilk instead of plain water for a chicken kitchen, which seasons and also gives flour something to grip. Dry: coarse salt over the skin, on a rack, uncovered in the fridge for several hours or overnight; the surface comes out matt and tight. Either way the wing goes into the oil dry, because water in hot oil is a hazard before it is a texture problem.
text.today: Standard in Southern fried chicken kitchens and in most home wing recipes; largely absent from the Buffalo account, which describes a wing fried straight. *Tradition holds —* a Buffalo house asked about brining tends to answer that it does nothing to the wing at all before the fryer.

names.name: the deep fryer
names.said: A bar counts its age in fryers. Forty years on one vat is a thing people say about a place before they say anything about the sauce.

text.what: The machine or pot the wing goes into: food submerged in hot fat rather than shallow-fried in a pan. A commercial vat, a chip pan, a wok, a Dutch oven or a cast-iron pot all do it. Industrially, a pressure fryer or a vacuum fryer may be used. Fry baskets contain the food in the fryer and strain it on the way out, and a thermometer is the other tool that matters.
text.story:
The physics is the reason the method works and the reason it burns people. Deep frying puts food in oil typically between 350 °F / 177 °C and 375 °F / 191 °C, though fryers can pass 400 °F / 205 °C. Hot oil heats the water inside the food and steams it; the vapour pushes outward and oil cannot travel against that flow, so as long as the oil is hot enough and the food is not in too long, penetration stays at the surface — foods deep-fried at proper temperatures absorb less than about 2 tbsp per 2.5 cups of oil used. Cook too long and the water is gone and the oil comes in.

The informal tests are older than the thermometers. A pinch of flour should sizzle without burning. A piece dropped in should sink a little and come back up: sinking without resurfacing means the oil is too cold, not sinking at all means it is too hot.

The pressure version runs a different physics. A pressure fryer is a pressure cooker filled with hot oil, so food cooks fast at high heat while keeping its water — the machine behind broasting, and behind the jojo.

*Inference —* the fryer is what made the wing a bar food rather than a kitchen food. It needs no cook watching a pan, it turns out a countable portion in minutes, and it will do fries, mozzarella sticks and pizza logs out of the same oil while it waits.
text.how: Bring the oil to temperature and hold it there; a basket of cold wings drops it, so fry in loads the vat can recover from. Dry the food before it goes in. Drain over the vat, not onto paper, or the crust steams itself soft. Strain solids out at the end of service — oil can be reused a few times after straining, and excessive reuse of the same oil breaks it down. Never water on an oil fire: water flashes to steam and throws burning oil in all directions, which is a slopover. Class F extinguisher, a lid, or a fire blanket; most commercial deep fryers carry automatic foam suppression.
text.today: Fast food is one of the most common ways deep-fried food is eaten in North America, and soybean oil is a popular medium there. *Tradition holds —* a shop's oil schedule is the thing regulars notice and never name; they say the wings taste different on a Tuesday.

names.name: the double fry
names.said: Fry, rest, fry. The rest is not a pause in the method; it is the method.

text.what: Frying in two passes with a rest between them. The first pass cooks the piece through and drives water out of the skin; the rest lets the surface dry and the interior even out; the second pass, hotter, builds the crust. The result is the thin, hard, glassy shell that will not go soft under sauce.
text.story:
Korean fried chicken is the tradition that made the method famous. Julia Moskin of The New York Times described it as having a "thin, crackly and almost transparent crust". Bonchon Chicken, founded in Busan in 2002 by Jinduk Seo, built a brand on it: its recipe cooks the chicken in two steps, the first until the fat from the skin is cooked off and the moisture is held in the meat, then a rest, then a second cook. That dehydration produces a thin crispy shell that acts as a protective layer against moisture getting back in. Because the shell is the product, Bonchon brushes sauce on by hand rather than tossing in containers, to spread it without wrecking the texture.

The potato got there first. French fries use the same architecture: a first bath at around 160 °C / 320 °F to cook the fries through, a second at 190 °C / 375 °F to crisp the exterior.

*Inference —* double frying and saucing are in tension. The method exists to make a crust that survives liquid; the Buffalo bowl exists to soak a crust in liquid. Shops that do both usually brush rather than toss, which is the argument sauce-on-the-side is having in a different accent.
text.how: Fry the first pass at a moderate heat until cooked through and the skin has given up its fat. Lift, drain and rest — minutes, not seconds, and uncovered, so steam leaves rather than condensing back. Second pass hotter and short, until the surface goes hard and the colour sets. Sauce after, brushed or tossed. Wings hold the rest well because they are small and the skin is most of the surface.
text.today: Standard at Korean fried chicken shops in the United States and in the chains that expanded out of a saturated home market — by 2026 South Korea had about 40,000 fried chicken restaurants, with 1,800 more run internationally by Korean brands in 60 countries. American bars borrow the method under the words extra crispy without always borrowing the rest.

names.name: the dredge
names.said: Three trays: flour, egg, crumb. One hand wet, one hand dry, or you end up with a glove.

text.what: Coating food before it fries. One common method for preparing food for deep frying involves adding multiple layers of batter around the food — cornmeal, flour or tempura — and breadcrumbs may be used. On a wing it is the difference between Buffalo and Rochester; on everything else at the counter it is simply how the thing is made.
text.story:
Every tradition at this counter has its own dredge. Nashville hot chicken is marinated in buttermilk to carry flavour and hold the meat's juices, then floured and fried, with the cayenne paste applied by the server afterward with a spoon and gloves. The mozzarella stick's Italian prototype, mozzarella milanese, is mozzarella dredged in flour, egg and breadcrumbs and pan-fried. John Young's Buffalo wings from 1961 were breaded, deep fried and served in a tomato-based mumbo sauce.

*Inference —* the three-stage dredge is a moisture problem solved in order. Flour dries the surface so egg will grip; egg is glue; crumb is the crust. Skip a stage and the coat slides off in the oil, which is why a station is set up as trays and not as a bowl.
text.how: Dry the pieces first; wet food sheds flour. Season the flour, not the meat, if the coat is the only seasoning going on. Flour, then egg, then crumb — one hand for dry trays and one for wet, or both hands cake. Rest the coated pieces a few minutes so the flour hydrates and bonds. Shake off surplus: loose flour burns in the oil and dirties the vat for the next load. A single flour dredge gives a thin crust; a double dip gives a craggy one.
text.today: Standard across American fried chicken, and the practice a Buffalo house defines itself against. *Tradition holds —* a shop's flour is the part of the recipe it will not discuss, and the part customers assume is a secret when it is often just flour, salt and pepper.

names.name: frying oil
names.said: Ask what a shop fries in and you learn more about the wings than the sauce list tells you.

text.what: What the wing is cooked in. Deep frying submerges food in hot fat — traditionally lard, today most commonly oil — and the choice of fat sets flavour, how long the vat lasts, what the shop pays and what goes on the allergen sheet. Four answers cover most American wing counters: beef tallow, peanut, soybean and canola.
text.story:
Beef fat has the oldest claim and the shortest modern run. Beef suet was recommended as superior in the older frying literature, and Belgian tradition requires fries be fried in filtered cattle fat — blanc de boeuf, ossewit. McDonald's used a mixture of 93% beef tallow and 7% cottonseed oil until 1990, when it switched to vegetable oil with beef flavouring. Horse fat was standard in northern France and Belgium until recently.

Soybean oil took the volume. In the United States especially, soybean oil is a popular medium in fast food, and fast food is one of the most common ways deep-fried food is eaten in North America. Trans fats appear in restaurant frying shortenings because they last longer than most conventional oils before going rancid; in the early 21st century non-hydrogenated vegetable oils with longer lifespans became available. Trans fat formed during frying increases with frying temperature, frying time, oil oxidation and oil reuse, and because chains use different fats in different locations, trans fat levels in fast food vary widely.

Canola is rapeseed. Many countries including the United Kingdom use pure or hydrogenated rapeseed oil for deep-frying; the Mediterranean tradition uses olive oil, and research indicates virgin olive oil is unusual among cooking oils for being very rich in monounsaturated fatty acids. Some studies have found frying in olive and sunflower oils less detrimental to health, and in some cases with positive effects on insulin levels.

*Tradition holds —* peanut oil is the fat American cooks name first for frying chicken and turkey, and the allergen is why plenty of shops will not keep it. This project has not found a cited source for either claim, and both are recorded here as unverified.

*Inference —* the argument over frying fat is the same argument the wing has everywhere else: the thing that makes it taste like itself is the thing a national menu has to answer for.
text.how: Hold the vat at 350–375 °F / 177–191 °C and let it recover between loads. Strain the solids at the end of service; oil can be reused a few times after straining, and excessive reuse breaks it down and releases compounds into the food. Some European countries set public health standards for frying-oil safety. Deep fat frying above 180 °C in the presence of moisture and air drives free radicals, oxidation, hydrolysis, isomerisation and polymerisation — water attacks the ester linkages of triacylglycerols, producing glycerol and free fatty acids, and those acids speed the reaction up. In practice that is what old oil tastes like.
text.today: Chains publish their frying fat and independents rarely do. *Inference —* a shop that runs one vat for wings, fries, mozzarella sticks and fish is selling the oil as much as the recipe, and regulars taste the schedule before they could name it.
