names.name: mumbo
names.said: Spelled mumbo in Chicago and on the trademark, mambo on plenty of D.C. carryout menus. Same sound.

etymology.root: no agreed etymon. As a commercial name the chain runs Argia B. Collins Sr.'s Chicago barbecue sauce → the registered mark MUMBO → the D.C. carryout word; the D.C. spelling mambo may be reshaping by the dance name
etymology.first_attested: 1950 as a trademark: Collins and his business used the Mumbo mark from at least as early as 1950, and his successor-in-interest Select Brands, LLC registered it with the USPTO on 25 May 1999, Registration No. 2,247,855
etymology.note: *Folk —* the mambo spelling invites a story about the dance, and the dance-named D.C. go-go group Mambo Sauce took its name from the condiment rather than the other way round. No source this project found derives the word from the dance, and none derives it from anywhere else either.

text.what: A word for a sweet-sour-hot red condiment, sold behind plexiglass in Washington carryouts and poured on fried wings, french fries, jumbo shrimp and fried rice. Barbecue-adjacent, sweeter than barbecue sauce, and by most accounts sourer or hotter as well; the recipe varies by counter.
text.story:
The word is in dispute, and the dispute is on the record. Argia B. Collins Sr. used Mumbo for a barbecue sauce at his Chicago restaurant from at least 1950; Select Brands, his successor-in-interest, holds the registration and has challenged D.C. uses of the name as infringing.

Washington tells it the other way. Capital City Mumbo Sauce dates the sauce to a restaurant called Wings-n-Things in the late 1960s. Complicating both, John Young was serving Mumbo sauce on chicken wings at John Young's Wings 'n Things in Buffalo from the early 1960s, and Young himself credited a Washington restaurant for the sauce. Because Collins's mark runs back to the 1950s, it has been argued that the D.C. sauce is the Chicago sauce transplanted. After two years of proceedings the Trademark Trial and Appeal Board found that a D.C.-based company could not take the name from its Chicago founder.

The argument is not only legal. In 2018 D.C. Mayor Muriel Bowser called Mumbo Sauce "annoying" in a Facebook post and questioned whether it was "quintessential" D.C.; her spokesperson said the remarks were meant to liven Thanksgiving discussions. On 9 October 2023 McDonald's released a version as a limited-time dipping sauce, with a short documentary about the sauce's history alongside it.
text.how: Asked for by the container: 'mumbo on the side', or poured over the box so the fries under the wings take it too.

names.name: naked
names.said: 'Naked or breaded?' — a question you hear where breading is the default, and almost never in Buffalo.

etymology.root: Old English nacod 'bare, unclothed' → Middle English naked; the menu sense is a metaphor, breading read as clothing
etymology.note: *Inference —* the word only exists because somewhere else is the default. A Buffalo bar has no use for it: its wings are unbreaded, so bare is the unmarked case and needs no name. Hooters, whose house style is hand-breaded, does need one, and prints it.

text.what: Unbreaded. A wing fried in nothing but its own skin, no flour, no batter, no dredge. Hooters, which breads by hand as its original style, lists the alternative as Naked Wings and describes them: "Traditional style. No breading, but just as good. Order them with your favorite Hooters wing sauce or rub."
text.how: Say it before the sauce: naked, hot, ranch. Naked skin crisps and then goes soft under sauce fast, so naked wings are tossed later and carried out quicker than breaded ones — which is the argument for eating them at the bar rather than in a box.

names.name: weck
names.said: Rhymes with deck. 'Beef on weck', never 'beef on a weck'.

etymology.root: German Weck 'bread roll' (the word of the southwestern dialects — Palatinate, Saarland, Baden, Swabia; northern Germans say Brötchen) ← Old High German wecki, weggi 'wedge; wedge-shaped baked good' ← Proto-West Germanic *wagi ← Proto-Germanic *wagjaz 'wedge'. The full compound is kummelweck: German Kümmel 'caraway' (← Middle High German kümel, kumel ← Old High German kumil ← Proto-West Germanic *kumil 'caraway, cumin seed') + Weck. So the name means, exactly, caraway roll — and the bread is a wedge before it is a roll.
etymology.note: *Tradition holds —* a German baker named William Wahr, thought to have come from the Black Forest, made the kummelweck in Buffalo, possibly working from the Swabian Schwäbische Seele, a thin salt-and-caraway loaf left as a ceremonial offering for the dead; a Western New York butcher puts the sandwich's creation in the mid-19th century. The record calls the sandwich's origin not well established, and this project leaves it there.

text.what: Half of a sandwich name that lost its other half. Weck is the kummelweck roll: kosher salt and caraway seeds baked onto the top, softer and fluffier than the German Kümmelbrötchen it descends from. Buffalo-area bakeries are the only commercial source for it. Beef on weck — rare roast beef, hand-carved thin, the top of the roll dipped in jus, horseradish spread to taste — is one of the three foods Buffalo is known for, with wings and sponge candy.
text.story:
The roll is a German loan that stopped travelling. Weck is a dialect word from southwestern Germany, carried to a Great Lakes port by German bakers and then fixed to one sandwich in one region, where it stayed. *Inference —* that is why it reads as a Buffalo word rather than a German one: outside western New York nobody has a use for it, so nobody borrowed it further.

It reached the wing world sideways. Buffalo Wild Wings was started by former western New Yorkers and opened as "Buffalo Wild Wings and Weck", abbreviated BW3 — the third W was the weck. The company dropped the W in 1998, and some people still say BW3 anyway. The chain used to serve an updated version of the sandwich called the Thirty-Fifth Weck Sandwich.
text.how: Ordered beside the wings, not instead of them: a Buffalo table that has ordered wings for the room orders a beef on weck for whoever did not want sauce on their hands. A pub owner is said to have used the salty roll to sell more drinks, which is the same trade a wing night makes.

names.name: wet and dry
names.said: 'Lemon pepper. Wet.' Two words after the flavour, and the order changes.

etymology.root: wet + dry, plain antonyms recruited as a pair of menu terms: wet = finished in a liquid sauce, dry = finished in a powder
etymology.note: The pair reached a national audience through Atlanta. 'Lemon pepper wet' was invented at the American Deli in Atlanta; the second episode of the television series Atlanta put it in a character's hands from J.R. Crickets, which had no such item, and J.R. Crickets added it to the menu in 2017 in the show's honour. *Inference —* the phrase was counter shorthand long before the show; the show is only the first dated place this project can point at.

text.what: A two-way choice about the finish, asked after you have picked a flavour. Dry means the cooked wing gets tossed in seasoning — powder on crust. Wet means it gets tossed in something liquid, so butter or sauce carries the same seasoning. Same flavour name, two different foods.
text.how: Order shape is flavour first, then the word: 'lemon pepper wet', 'hot lemon pepper dry'. Some Atlanta counters build wet by tossing in butter or buffalo sauce and then hitting the wings with dry seasoning anyway, which is a third thing with a two-word name. Dry travels better in a box; wet goes soft.

text.what: A weekly price special on wings, usually sold by the piece and usually paired with a drink minimum. The deal is the draw; the pitcher is the margin.
text.how: Which night? No single one owns it. Buffalo Wing Guide, which keeps a running list of western New York specials, files them under Monday through Sunday plus Every Day — every weekday carries some. A bar-marketing write-up describes the pull the other way round, saying wing night is what "makes a bar busy on Monday or Tuesday night". So the answer is that wing night lands where the week is slow, and the name it gets depends on which letter it can rhyme with.
text.today: Buffalo Wing Guide's 2026 list warns that "all wing specials and pricing are subject to change. Please call bar or restaurant to verify accuracy" — which is the state of every posted wing price after three years of wing costs moving.

etymology.root: wing + tip, a plain compound; the piece also answers to flapper and to pointer, and all three names describe the same shape from a different angle
etymology.note: Wikipedia's Buffalo wing article names the three segments "drumette, flat, and flapper or pointer"; its poultry article gives "the wing tip (also called the 'flapper')". *Inference —* tip is what a butcher calls it, flapper what a cook calls it, pointer what a diner calls it when handed one.

text.what: Third segment, the pointed end. Skin, cartilage, two slivers of bone, almost no meat. Usually cut off before the wing reaches a fryer and boiled into stock instead, though some restaurants serve it still joined to the flat.
text.how: Where it survives on the plate, it is eaten whole — crust, cartilage and all — or left in the bone bowl. Where it does not, it goes into a stockpot: collagen from the joints is what makes chicken stock set, so the least saleable piece of the wing is the one worth most to a kitchen that makes its own.

text.what: Buffalo paints its own story on its walls, and the wing is part of what gets painted. The city's public art runs from commissioned murals on Main Street and Hertel Avenue to neighbourhood walls raised by crowdfunding, and at least one of them exists to settle an argument: in November 2021 a mural went up at Jefferson and Carlton, on the corner where John Young's Wings 'n Things stood, recreating the artwork that had hung inside his shop. The murals are copyrighted by the people who painted them, and one Buffalo muralist has invoiced businesses for using images of his wall, which is why this page names walls and does not reproduce them.

sections.text:
It stands at Jefferson Avenue and Carlton Street, the site of John Young's first restaurant. John Baker and the WNY Urban Arts Collective installed it in November 2021, recreating an original work by William Cooper and Dalton Easton that had hung inside the Wings 'n Things shop.

Buffalo Bike Tours raised more than $12,000 for it — a GoFundMe, chicken wing pop-up events, and grants from the Baird Foundation and the Buffalo Niagara Medical Campus. Marc Moscato said the effort would add "solar lights and interpretative signage in the coming weeks" and planned "a public celebration in the spring, with a memorial bike ride to kick of Buffalo Bike Tours 2022 season." Members of Young's family stood with the supporters at the unveiling.

*Inference —* the wall does a job no paper in the origin argument does. Young's claim has no menu, no receipt and no trademark behind it; it has a corner, and now the corner is marked.

Casey William Milbrand painted Greetings from Buffalo on Ellicott Street in 2016, in the form of a large-letter postcard — a twelve-pointed sun rising behind a red and purple skyline on a field of blue squares. Visit Buffalo helped promote it. It became the city's most photographed wall.

Milbrand is a Buffalo native with a BS in architecture from the University at Buffalo and an MA from the Illinois Institute of Technology.

sections.h: Who owns a photograph of a wall
sections.text:
In April 2023 Spectrum News 1 Buffalo reported that Milbrand had been invoicing businesses that used images of the mural commercially, including a $5,000 invoice sent to Buffalo Bike Tours on 3 April, and a settlement for what the report calls a modest amount with Roswell Park Comprehensive Cancer Center after court action. His attorney Stuart Shapiro said commercial use requires permission and that invoices may be sent without a prior cease-and-desist.

Milbrand's own statement, as reported: "You are also free to reach out directly to an artist if you want to use their copyrighted art for commercial purposes. It's just good business practice." Marc Moscato of Buffalo Bike Tours disputed the characterisation: "There's nothing malicious. I'm not monetizing in any way."

*Inference —* the episode is the reason this site links to Buffalo's walls rather than reproducing them. A photograph of a mural is two works. The photographer can license one of them.

sections.h: What the genre does for a city
sections.text:
*Tradition holds —* a mural is the cheapest large claim a neighbourhood can make. It needs a wall, a permission, a lift and a fortnight, and it does not go through a planning process the way a monument does. Buffalo's run to civic self-portraiture: the name of the city in large letters, the grain elevators, the skyline, the bison, and the wing.

Visit Buffalo publishes a neighbourhood guide to the city's public art, which puts the murals on the same footing as the Wing Trail — a marketing list that also functions as the nearest thing to a register.

*Inference —* the wing turns up in Buffalo's murals in two modes, and they are different arguments. One is the city's badge: a wing used the way the bison and the grain elevator are used, as a shorthand for the place, on a wall that is about Buffalo rather than about food. The other is specific and contested — a wall that names a person, a corner and a year, and by doing so takes a side in who invented the dish. Only the second kind carries a date and a claim.

sections.h: Paint, and how long it lasts
sections.text: *Tradition holds —* exterior mural work is acrylic or elastomeric wall paint, sprayed and brushed, usually over a primed and sometimes a rendered surface, and finished with a UV-resistant clear coat. Red and orange pigments — the wing's own colours — fade first and hardest in sunlight, which is why a wing mural looks older faster than the blues beside it. Maintenance is the artist's if anybody's, and mostly it is nobody's.

text.what: The sign over a wing or fried-chicken counter is a working document. It has to be readable from a car at thirty miles an hour, name the shop, say CHICKEN, and usually price something. It comes in two families that overlap: brush-lettered paint, on plywood, on stucco, on the window glass itself; and the internally lit plastic box with changeable letters underneath. The cartoon bird is optional and very common. Almost none of it is signed, almost all of it is made locally, and it is replaced rather than restored, which is why the record of it is photographic.

sections.h: What the sign has to do
sections.text:
Four jobs, in order of size. Say the name. Say CHICKEN, or WINGS, in the largest letters on the panel — because the category sells before the name does. Price something, usually one combination, because a price is what makes a driver slow down. Point: an arrow, a hand, or an ORDER HERE over the window.

*Inference —* the hierarchy is why so many of these signs look alike across cities that share nothing else. The constraints are the same in Chicago, Atlanta, Nashville and Washington, and they produce the same layout.

*Tradition holds —* the hand-painted counter sign is sign-painter's work: one-shot enamel, a lettering quill, a chalk snap line, and a shop's name laid out to fill the board rather than to fit a typeface. The tells are the ones the trade knows — brush-modulated strokes, letters that widen where the space allows, a drop shadow painted in a second pass, and spacing decided by eye.

The same hand usually does the menu board inside: the list over the counter, the prices painted and then repainted over as they move, so an old price shows through a new one. That layering is the only dated thing in most of these shops.

The illuminated plastic-faced cabinet arrived with the postwar strip and did not leave. A translucent face, fluorescent tubes behind it, the shop's name silkscreened or vinyl-cut onto the plastic, and beneath it a changeable-copy reader board with black letters slid into tracks.

It is the cheapest way to be visible after dark, which is when a wing counter does much of its business, and the reader board gives a shop something it cannot get any other way: copy it can change this afternoon. WINGS 10 PC, or the specials, or a message about the football.

A chicken drawn as a character — upright, often wearing a chef's hat or an apron, sometimes carrying a tray, frequently pointing at the shop's own name. *Tradition holds —* the joke is old and untroubled: the bird recommends its own cooking.

It shares its grammar with the rooster weathervane and with barbecue's pig: an animal rendered as a sign for the place that sells it, drawn friendly rather than lifelike, and used as a mark a customer can recognise before reading a word.

Chiefly in two public photographic collections, both at the Library of Congress and both public domain, which is why this site can point at them.

John Margolies spent decades photographing American roadside architecture; his chicken signs on Wikimedia Commons include a 1979 chicken sign in El Paso, Texas, Cohen's Chicken House in Junction City, Kansas, Dario Chicken In-The Box in Rutherfordton, North Carolina, and the Chicken In the Rough restaurant sign on Route 11 in New Market, Virginia. Carol M. Highsmith's Library of Congress work covers the same ground later, including a Lucy's Fried Chicken sign on Burnet Road in Austin, Texas, photographed in April 2014.

*Inference —* the collections skew to what a photographer driving a highway could see. Counter signs on a city block, inside a neighbourhood, photograph worse and survive in the record less.

Vinyl cut on a plotter and applied to an acrylic face. Channel letters in aluminium with LED modules behind them, which replaced neon on cost rather than on looks. Full-colour printed banners for a new flavour, zip-tied over the old sign and left up for years. Menu boards as backlit translucent prints in a rail, so one panel can be swapped when a price moves.

The hand-painted window is not gone. It persists where a shop's landlord will not permit a cabinet, where the budget is a weekend, and where a shop wants to look like it has been there longer than it has.

sections.h: Reading one before you go in
sections.text: *Tradition holds —* the sign tells you the shop's shape. An ORDER HERE window with a speaker means no dining room. Prices painted rather than printed mean they do not change often. A reader board with three different letter heights means the letters ran out. Hours hand-lettered on the glass, rather than printed on a decal, usually means the hours are the owner's and negotiable.

text.what: A hot sauce label sells one thing before it sells any other: how much it will hurt. The genre has a settled vocabulary — devils, flames, skulls, warning text set like a hazard placard, a name that is a dare, and often a number. Beneath the artwork the same panel carries what federal law requires, including an ingredient list in descending order by weight, which is why this site can read a bottle's ingredient rank off a photograph of its back. The front is a promise. The back is a fact.

sections.text:
*Tradition holds —* the front panel works a short list of devices. A devil, horned and usually cheerful. Flame, as a border, a background, or lettering on fire. A skull, sometimes with the pepper in its teeth. A pepper drawn as a character. Warning type in a yellow-and-black band, borrowed from industrial hazard signage. A name doing the dare — atomic, ghost, reaper, death, insanity.

The register is comic rather than frightening, and deliberately so: the buyer is being invited to take a risk that is safe.

sections.h: The number, and when it means anything
sections.text:
Scoville heat units get printed on labels as a headline figure. A Scoville number is only worth something where somebody publishes the measurement and says who made it, which is why this site records a scoville value on a sauce only where a maker or a lab publishes one, and never estimates it.

What a label always does carry is the maker's own heat word — mild, medium, hot, extra hot, atomic — and this site records that verbatim, as the maker's claim rather than as a measurement.

The oldest American brands keep old labels on purpose. Tabasco, from the McIlhenny Company, appeared in 1868 and is the earliest recognisable brand in the US hot sauce trade; its diamond label, small bottle and green cap are effectively unchanged as design elements. Frank's RedHot's 1965 label survives as an image on Wikimedia Commons under CC BY-SA 4.0.

*Inference —* a heritage label is an argument about age in the same way a wing shop's hand-painted window is. It says the recipe has not moved. Whether the recipe has moved is a separate question the label does not answer.

*Tradition holds —* a category of label exists for sauces that are not really condiments: extract sauces sold as an ordeal, in small bottles, often with a coffin, a skull-shaped bottle, or a wax seal, and with copy that instructs the buyer to use one drop. They are the bottled version of the extra-hot wing challenge a bar runs with a photograph on the wall for whoever finishes.

The design signals the change of category. A sauce meant for food gets a food label; a sauce meant for a dare gets packaging borrowed from poisons and from heavy metal record sleeves.

sections.h: What the back panel must say
sections.text:
The regulated side. An ingredient list in descending order by weight, a net quantity, a nutrition panel with a stated serving size, the maker's name and place, and allergen information where it applies.

That ordering requirement is what makes a label usable as data. Read the list and you know whether the sauce leads with peppers, with vinegar, with tomato or with sugar, which is more informative about how it will taste than anything on the front. This site's sauce profiles are built out of exactly that: ingredient rank in label order, plus sodium and sugar per tablespoon from the panel.

*Inference —* hot sauce is merchandised in a way that pushes the labels toward shouting. It sits in a long row of small bottles, most of a similar shape, at a similar price, where the whole differentiation happens in about four inches of front panel viewed at arm's length. That is a harder design brief than a wing counter's sign has, and it explains the volume of the graphics better than any claim about the buyers does.

text.what: A chicken drawn in bent glass tube, filled with gas, and run off a transformer over a bar, a drive-in or a wing counter. The bird is usually animated in the cheap way neon animates: two or three sets of tubes switched in sequence so a wing flaps, steam rises, or an arrow chases. Neon signs are made by hand, by a bender working a ribbon burner, which is why a town's neon looks like the shops of the two or three benders who worked there. They are expensive to build, expensive to repair, and the first thing an owner replaces when a tube goes, which is why the surviving ones are mostly in cities that decided to protect them.

sections.text:
*Tradition holds —* a neon sign starts as a full-size drawing on fireproof paper. The bender heats soft glass tube over a ribbon burner and works it against the pattern, bend by bend, blowing gently to keep the bore open. Electrodes go on the ends; the tube is pumped down, bombarded to drive out impurities, and filled — neon for red and orange, argon with a drop of mercury for blue, and coloured or phosphor-coated glass for everything else. A transformer supplies the high voltage.

A chicken is a hard shape for it. Curves in tube have a minimum radius, so a bird's beak, comb and tail feathers get simplified until they read at fifty feet — which is the reason neon birds look like each other. The medium does the stylising.

sections.h: Why a bird, and why lit
sections.text:
Neon belongs to the hours a wing counter works. It is legible from a road after dark, it needs no separate illumination, and it holds colour in rain in a way a painted panel does not.

*Inference —* the bird is the same bird as on the painted signs, and for the same reason: the shop is selling a category before it sells a name. Lighting it changes the register rather than the message. A lit chicken over a door reads as open, which a painted one never can.

*Tradition holds —* neon animates by switching rather than by moving. Two wing positions on separate circuits, flashed alternately, make a bird flap. Three arrows lit in sequence pull the eye toward a door. Steam is three curls that light bottom to top. The controller is a rotating drum or, later, a solid-state flasher, and the whole vocabulary is about a dozen tricks long.

It is the animation that dates a sign more precisely than the lettering does, because a flasher is a component with a period.

Over the door of a corner bar, in the window beside the beer signs, on a pylon at a drive-in, and along a commercial strip where the sign has to compete with the sign next door. The wing counter's neon is usually small and in the window — OPEN, WINGS, the bird — rather than a pole sign, because the shop rents a storefront and cannot put anything on the roof.

Neon dies by degrees. A cracked tube goes dark and gets left dark; the electrode fails and the section stays out; the transformer hums and gets unplugged. A bender has to come, which costs more than a printed banner over the whole thing.

*Inference —* that economics, more than taste, is why neon retreated. LED channel letters and flexible LED tube do a passable imitation for a fraction of the maintenance, and most of what reads as neon on a wing counter in 2026 is LED.

The public photographic record is thinner than the painted-sign record. Carol M. Highsmith photographed a neon sign at a Lucy's Fried Chicken on Burnet Road in Austin, Texas in April 2014, and the image is public domain through the Library of Congress; museum neon exhibits and civic sign parks account for much of the rest on Wikimedia Commons.

*Tradition holds —* an old neon sign outlives the business under it more often than not. It gets sold with the building, adopted by the next tenant, bought by a collector, or taken into a museum. A chicken that once advertised a fry counter can end up over a bar that serves no chicken at all, which is how a sign becomes a piece of furniture.

text.what: A rooster cut or moulded in sheet metal, balanced on a spindle, and put on a roof to show which way the wind blows. It is the oldest American use of a chicken as a public sign, it predates every wing counter by centuries, and the shape it settled into — flat body, raised comb, fanned tail, one leg forward — is the same silhouette a fried chicken sign draws today. American vanes were made in copper and zinc by nineteenth-century firms working from moulds, and museums now hold them as folk sculpture; the Smithsonian American Art Museum has released photographs of several under CC0.

sections.text:
A vane is a shape mounted off-centre on a vertical spindle so the wind turns the larger surface downwind and the smaller end points into it. The rooster's tail is the sail; the head is the pointer. Beneath it sit the fixed direction letters, N, S, E, W, on rods.

It is a working instrument before it is decoration, and the shape has to earn its aerodynamics: the tail has to be broad, the body flat, the whole thing light enough to turn in a light breeze and strong enough to survive a gale.

sections.h: How the bird got up there
sections.text:
*Tradition holds —* the cockerel came to European roofs through the church, where a weathercock on a steeple carried a religious reading, and the practice moved to civic and farm buildings and then across the Atlantic. The detail of that history is not something this project has sourced; what is documented is the American object that resulted.

*Inference —* by the time the rooster reaches an American barn it is no longer making an argument about anything. It is a shape everybody recognises at a distance, which is the only quality a roof ornament needs.

Nineteenth-century American vanes were commonly made of sheet copper hammered into carved wooden moulds in two halves and soldered together, sometimes gilded, sometimes zinc-headed for weight, and mounted on an iron rod. Some were carved in wood and cut in flat sheet iron by a local smith.

The Smithsonian American Art Museum holds rooster vanes of this kind — its nineteenth-century examples are catalogued to anonymous makers — and has released images under CC0 through the Smithsonian Open Access programme, which is why they can be shown here and most later signage cannot.

sections.h: The silhouette, and where it went next
sections.text:
*Inference —* compare a copper vane to a painted chicken on a fry counter's sign and the drawing is nearly the same: body in profile, comb and wattles exaggerated so they read at distance, tail fanned to fill the space, legs simplified to two strokes. The vane's constraints produced that shape — it had to be flat, balanced and legible from the ground — and the sign painter inherited it, because the sign has the same problem.

The difference is what the bird is claiming. On a barn it points at the weather. Over a fry counter it points at the menu.

sections.h: Weather, and what a vane cannot do
sections.text:
A vane gives direction and nothing else. It does not measure speed, it lags in gusts, and it reads the wind at roof height rather than at ground level, which on a built-up street is a different wind altogether.

*Tradition holds —* farmers read them in combination with everything else they watched, and a vane's value was that it was visible from the field without going anywhere.

*Tradition holds —* old American vanes moved from roofs into the folk art market over the twentieth century, which pulled them off buildings and into rooms, and produced a reproduction trade making new vanes with artificial weathering. A vane indoors is a sculpture; a vane outdoors is an instrument; the same object is being valued for two different things, and the price is set by the first.

text.what: A wing festival poster does four things at once: names the event, fixes the date and the gate, lists the sponsors in descending size, and supplies a mascot the event can print on a T-shirt. The National Buffalo Wing Festival, founded in Buffalo in 2002 and held on Labor Day weekend, is the genre's anchor; Philadelphia's Wing Bowl, run by a radio station from 1993 to 2018, produced the same artwork in a louder register. The art is commercial, it is dated by design, and almost none of it is free to reuse — which is why this page describes it rather than shows it.

sections.h: The event the posters are for
sections.text:
The National Buffalo Wing Festival was inaugurated in 2002 at Sahlen Field in Buffalo and runs on Labor Day weekend. Drew Cerza founded it; the Buffalo News called him the Wing King. It culminates in a sanctioned wing-eating contest held on the Sunday every year since 2003 apart from 2020. It was held at Highmark Stadium from 2021 through the 2024 edition and returned to Sahlen Field in 2025.

Jill Greenburg's account of why it lasted, quoted in the festival's own record: "Of local festivals that have come and gone, the Wing Fest's staying power is a result of raising approximately $200,000 for local charities and serving almost 3,000,000 chicken wings with 100 sauce varieties to over 500,000 hungry visitors over the years."

sections.h: What has to fit on the sheet
sections.text:
Title. Year, often in Roman numerals if the event has run long enough to make a point of it. Dates and gate times. Venue. Ticket price or the words FREE ADMISSION. A sponsor block, which on a festival poster is not decoration but the reason the poster exists — the beer brand, the hot sauce brand, the local supermarket, the radio station, each sized by what it paid.

*Inference —* everything left over is the artwork, which is why festival posters are mostly type with one image, and why the image is almost always the mascot rather than a photograph of food.

*Tradition holds —* the visual kit is small and stable. A wing drawn with a face or with sunglasses. Flame, as an outline behind the type. A crown, because somebody is being crowned. A pepper as a punctuation mark. A bib. Colours run to the red-orange of the sauce against black or white, and the type is heavy, condensed, and often slanted to suggest speed.

Competitive eating brings its own iconography: the numbered placard, the table with the plates in a row, the timer, the mound. Wing Bowl's promotional art worked this hardest — an arena event with entrants who arrived with entourages, and artwork built on wrestling and boxing posters rather than on food photography.

The county fair poster, the chilli cook-off flyer, the crawfish boil, the rib burn-off, the state barbecue championship. They share the sponsor block, the mascot and the date-first hierarchy, and they share a production route: a local designer, a short run, and a shirt printed from the same file.

*Inference —* the poster is rarely the main artefact. The shirt is. A festival poster is designed knowing it will be cropped to a square for a shirt front and to a banner for a stage, which flattens the composition and pushes the mascot to the centre.

sections.h: What is free, and what is not
sections.text:
Almost none of it. Festival artwork is commissioned work, owned by the festival or its agency, and sponsor logos are trademarks on top of that. Wikimedia Commons holds photographs taken at the events — a 2012 shot of Joey Chestnut competing at the National Buffalo Wing Festival, released under CC BY 2.0 by the photographer, and crowd pictures from the same years — but not the poster art itself.

So this page names what the genre does and points at the photographs. *Inference —* that limit is typical of commercial vernacular art: the thing is everywhere and reproducible almost nowhere.

text.what: On 25 July 2024 the Supreme Court of Ohio held, 4 to 3, that a diner who swallowed a chicken bone from a boneless wing could not take his negligence claim to a jury, because he could reasonably have guarded against it. The case is Berkheimer v. REKM, L.L.C., 2024-Ohio-2787, 177 Ohio St.3d 431, docket 2023-0293. The majority wrote that calling the item a boneless wing described a cooking style. The dissent called that reasoning jabberwocky, twice. The argument the case dropped into is older than the case and older than the menu category: a boneless wing is breast meat, battered and fried, and the federal standard that governs what may be labelled a wing does not cover a restaurant menu at all.

sections.h: The case, and what is in the record
sections.text:
Michael Berkheimer ate boneless wings at Wings on Brookwood in 2016. A bone roughly five centimetres long lodged in his oesophagus, tearing it; infection followed in his thoracic cavity, and with it fever and difficulty breathing. He sued the restaurant, its food supplier and a chicken farm in negligence and breach of warranty. The trial court granted summary judgment to the defendants; the Supreme Court of Ohio affirmed on 25 July 2024, 4 to 3.

Justice Joseph T. Deters wrote for the majority. Justice Michael P. Donnelly wrote the dissent. Ohio applies a reasonable-expectation test: whether a consumer could reasonably have expected the injurious substance in the food and so could have guarded against it.

*Inference —* one caution about this page. The court's own PDF of the opinion was unreachable from this project on 16 September 2026, as were the Justia and CourtListener copies; the quotations below are reproduced from reporting that printed them, and each is attributed to the outlet that printed it. Anyone relying on the exact wording should read the slip opinion.

On the bone itself, Holland & Knight quotes the majority: "Like the oyster shell at issue in Allen, it is apparent that the bone ingested by Berkheimer was so large relative to the size of the food item he was eating that, as a matter of law, he reasonably could have guarded against it."

On the word on the menu, the same passage is quoted by Holland & Knight and by Reason's Volokh Conspiracy: "it is common sense that that label was merely a description of the cooking style."

The holding is about tort liability under Ohio's reasonable-expectation test. It is not a ruling about labelling, about advertising, or about what a restaurant may print.

Justice Donnelly's dissent is quoted by Reason's Volokh Conspiracy: "The result in this case is another nail in the coffin of the American jury system"; "More utter jabberwocky"; and, on the majority's cooking-style reading, "Jabberwocky. There is, of course, no authority for this assertion, because no sensible person has ever" — the post's excerpt breaks there.

On what a diner understands, he is quoted: "When they read the word 'boneless,' they think that it means 'without bones,' as do all sensible people." CBS News prints a further line: "Does anyone really believe that the parents in this country who feed their young children boneless wings...expect bones to be in the chicken?"

The dissent's complaint is procedural as much as lexical: that the question of what a diner could reasonably expect is a jury's to answer, and the majority took it away.

sections.h: What a boneless wing is made of
sections.text:
Breast meat. Russ Whitman, a poultry analyst at Urner Barry, told The Counter in February 2018 how it is done: "they take a piece of breast meat, and they essentially strip it down, cut it into five three-inch long pieces, and coat it with buffalo sauce, and throw it in a fryer." Asked whether it is a wing, he said: "I mean, no, it's not a wing at all. It's white meat, it's breast meat. Is it fair? I don't know what the rules are. It's misleading."

The process is the chicken nugget's process, which Robert C. Baker worked out at Cornell in the 1950s and published unpatented: coat the meat so it holds together, then batter it so the coating survives frying and freezing. A boneless wing is that, cut larger and sauced.

Wings got expensive and some diners wanted a neater thing to eat. Restaurants answered with a menu line called boneless wings — skinless boneless breast, floured and spiced, fried or baked, and sauced the same way the bone-in ones are. Sometimes it was sold under the spelling wyngz.

By the National Chicken Council's figures as reported by The Counter in 2018, traditional wings still accounted for 64% of all wings served in restaurants, with boneless orders falling that year. Datassential has since projected boneless growing on menus while bone-in stays flat. *Inference —* a category that is 36% of a market and growing is not a fringe; it is half the argument's reason for existing.

The federal standard is narrow. 9 CFR 381.170(b)(7): "'Wings' shall include the entire wing with all muscle and skin tissue intact, except that the wingtip may be removed." A poultry product that is not that may not be labelled a wing.

So when Nestlé wanted to put boneless chicken pieces in a DiGiorno frozen pizza box in 2011, USDA's Food Safety and Inspection Service offered a spelling instead. Consumer Reports, writing on 3 February 2011, reported the terms: "The FSIS allows the use of the term 'wyngz' to denote a product that is in the shape of a wing or a bite-size appetizer type product under the following conditions" — among them that the poultry is white chicken and that the product contains no wing meat — and that the agency stipulates "no other misspellings are permitted." Stephen Colbert put the spelling on television, which is how most people heard of it.

The rule reaches a package. It does not reach a menu: FSIS and FDA labelling standards govern what is printed on a label, and a restaurant's menu board is not one. *Inference —* that gap is the whole reason the question reached a court as a tort claim rather than a labelling complaint.

*Tradition holds —* people were saying a boneless wing is not a wing long before 2024 and long before wyngz. The sentence gets said across a bar counter and in the comments under every wing post, and it takes two forms that are worth keeping apart: a claim about anatomy, which is simply correct — breast is not wing — and a claim about worth, which is a preference. The court decided neither.

sections.h: What the decision does and does not settle
sections.text: It settles that in Ohio, a plaintiff in Berkheimer's position does not reach a jury on those facts. *Inference —* it does not define the word boneless, it does not bind any other state, it does not touch federal labelling, and it does not stop a restaurant calling the item whatever it likes. What it did do is hand both sides of a bar argument a court citation, which is why it is quoted far more often than it is read.

text.what: Every map, price, coordinate and recipe on this site comes from somewhere a reader can go and check. This page names each archive, dataset, directory and licence, says what it is good for, says what it will not tell you, and names the ones this project could not get into. Licences are quoted from the publisher's own terms. Dates are the dates I read them, which for all of these is 16 September 2026.

sections.text:
Licence: the Open Data Commons Open Database License, ODbL 1.0. The project's own terms require two things of a reuser — credit OpenStreetMap by displaying its attribution notice, and make clear that the data is available under the Open Database License — and add the share-alike condition: alter or build on the data and you may distribute the result only under the same licence.

Good for: a bar's coordinates, its street address, sometimes its opening days, sometimes its cuisine tag. It is the source behind the pins on this site's maps.

Will not tell you: whether a place is any good, whether it is still trading, or whether the hours are current. The data is edited by volunteers, a closed shop can sit on the map for years, and a shop that never got mapped is simply absent. An absence in OpenStreetMap is not evidence a place does not exist.

Licence: public domain. Used here for the Admin 1 states-and-provinces layer at 1:50 million, which is what draws the state outlines on the map.

Good for: country and state shapes, coastlines, lakes, at a scale that renders fast and small.

Will not tell you: anything at city scale. At 1:50m a county is a few pixels and a neighbourhood does not exist.

Licence: a work of the United States government, public domain. It carries branded-food label panels — the ingredient list in label order, serving size, sodium, sugars — alongside standard-reference and survey food data.

Good for: reading a bottled sauce the way its own label states it, which is how every sauce profile on this site records ingredient rank, sodium per tablespoon and sugar per tablespoon.

Will not tell you: what is in a house sauce. A bar's recipe is not on a label, and most of the sauces that matter most on this site are made in a kitchen, not a bottling plant.

Licence: US government work, public domain. Two weekly reports do the work here. The Weekly National Chicken Report (AMS_3646) gives wholesale parts prices in cents per pound with ranges, weighted averages and volumes. The Weekly Grocery Store Chicken Feature Activity report (AMS_2756) gives advertised retail prices in dollars per pound with the number of sampled stores behind each one, gathered from store circulars, newspaper ads and retailer websites.

Good for: a price with a date, a method and a sample size — the kind of number that can be quoted without hedging.

Will not tell you: what a flat costs as against a drumette. The wholesale report prices Wings – Whole and stops; the retail report bundles Party Wings, Flats and Drums into one line. It is also a weekly snapshot, not a series: a run of years has to be assembled week by week.

Licence: US government work, public domain, readable in full at the eCFR. 9 CFR 381.170(b) is the section that matters to wings: it defines Wings, Wing drummette and Wing portion, and it is quoted verbatim in two of this site's stories.

Good for: settling what a word means on a package.

Will not tell you: what a word means on a menu. The federal poultry standards govern labels. A restaurant's menu board is not a label, which is the gap that sent the boneless-wing argument to a tort court instead of a regulator.

Licence: varies by file, but Commons accepts only free content — material anyone may use for any purpose, including commercially and in derivative works. Non-commercial-only and no-derivatives licences are refused, and the policy states plainly that Commons does not accept content under the condition of fair use.

Good for: photographs with a licence attached to the file. Two public collections carry most of the American roadside material this site's art pages point at: John Margolies's roadside photographs at the Library of Congress and Carol M. Highsmith's, both public domain, and the Smithsonian American Art Museum's open-access releases under CC0.

Will not tell you: whether you may use the picture for everything. A free licence covers copyright and nothing else — personality rights, trademarks and the rights in whatever the photograph depicts survive it. A photograph of a mural is two works, and the mural's copyright is not the photographer's to license.

Licence: CC BY-SA 4.0. Reusable in full, with attribution, and only under the same licence.

Good for: recipe text this site can print whole rather than reducing to an ingredient list. Public-domain American cookbooks printed before 1930 travel the same way.

Will not tell you: how a particular shop does it. A community recipe is a method, not a provenance, and this site treats it as one.

Licence: none — a trade association's website, free to read, not free to redistribute. It represents producers and processors accounting for about 95% of US chicken production, and it lobbies Congress and the federal agencies.

Good for: the Chicken Wing Report each January, the Super Bowl consumption estimate that every newspaper reprints, and the Harris Poll dip and flavour questions it commissions, which are the only public numbers on ranch against blue cheese at the wing counter.

Will not tell you: how the estimate was made. The releases publish the figure and not the method. They are also an industry's own numbers about its own product, which is not a reason to discard them and is a reason to say whose they are every time.

Licence: none — a destination marketing organisation's webpage, free to read, not an open dataset. It names fourteen stops across Buffalo, Amherst, Getzville, Williamsville, East Aurora, Hamburg and Orchard Park, and sorts them by wing style.

Good for: a named, dated list of which shops the city itself puts forward, which this site records as a recognition rather than a ranking.

Will not tell you: who was left off, or why. A trail is a promotion. Inclusion measures attention paid, and nothing about the wings.

Licence: rights held by the Southern Foodways Alliance, an institute of the Center for the Study of Southern Culture at the University of Mississippi. Interviews — audio and transcripts — are free to read and listen to online. Using the material in research, scholarship, artistic production or publication requires permission from SFA first.

Good for: cooks and owners in their own recorded words, including the Nashville hot chicken kitchens this site's Tennessee records lean on. The interviews are dated and the interviewer is named, which is more provenance than most food writing carries.

Will not tell you: anything you may quote at length without asking. Free to read is not free to reuse, and this site cites these interviews rather than reproducing them.

Licence: a judicial opinion of a US court is a public record and carries no copyright. Berkheimer v. REKM, L.L.C., 2024-Ohio-2787, 177 Ohio St.3d 431, docket 2023-0293, decided 25 July 2024, is the one this site leans on.

Good for: exact words, attributed to the judge who wrote them, in a document that will still be there next year.

Will not tell you: anything, if you cannot fetch it. On 16 September 2026 the Supreme Court of Ohio's own PDF refused this project's connection, and the Justia, CourtListener and FindLaw copies returned 403 or a challenge page. The quotations on that story are therefore taken from reporting that printed them, and are labelled that way.

sections.h: What this project could not get into
sections.text:
Named plainly, because a gap that is not named looks like a decision.

Calvin Trillin's An Attempt to Compile a Short History of the Buffalo Chicken Wing, The New Yorker, 25 August 1980. In copyright and behind the magazine's paywall. It is cited throughout as the source of Dominic Bellissimo's midnight telling, and quoted only at the length that reporting about it quotes.

The FSIS Food Standards and Labeling Policy Book, which carries the wyngz policy in the agency's own words. The USDA servers returned 403 to every request on 16 September 2026, so the policy is quoted from Consumer Reports quoting FSIS.

Urner Barry's poultry price series, the one the trade actually uses to price a flat against a drumette. Subscription only.

Circana and NielsenIQ retail scanner data, which would show ranch and blue cheese dollar sales side by side. Subscription only.

Restaurant menus. The Buffalo shops' own prices sit behind ordering platforms that serve nothing to a plain request; Bar-Bill and Duff's both refused on 16 September 2026.

Mural photographs. Buffalo's murals are copyrighted by the artists who painted them, and at least one Buffalo muralist has invoiced businesses for commercial use of images of his wall. This site links to murals and does not reproduce them.

text.what: Buffalo sends out blue cheese. America buys ranch. Blue cheese reached the wing plate on the first night of the Anchor Bar story, off the antipasto tray, and it is still the house cup along the city's wing trail. Ranch was invented by a plumbing contractor named Steve Henson in the early 1950s, sold by mail from a Santa Barbara County guest ranch from 1957, bought by Clorox in 1972, and has outsold every other salad dressing in the United States since 1992. Asked what they eat wings with, more Americans say ranch than say blue cheese, by roughly two to one in the trade association's own polling. Both numbers and both dips are set out below, with whose figures they are and when they were taken.

sections.h: What Buffalo puts on the plate
sections.text: The Anchor Bar's account has Teressa Bellissimo sending the first wings out with celery and blue cheese taken from the bar's antipasto tray. Nothing about that was a decision about dips; it was what the kitchen had. Sixty years on it is the house standard: a medium order in Buffalo arrives with celery, carrots and a cup of chunky blue cheese whether or not anybody asked.

Blue cheese dressing runs blue cheese, mayonnaise, and buttermilk, sour cream, yogurt or milk, with vinegar, onion powder and garlic powder. There is also a vinaigrette version — oil, blue cheese, vinegar, seasonings — that is not what comes in the cup. It separates: oil and water coming apart is a known problem with the emulsion, and the organisms that spoil salad dressings, Saccharomyces bailii and Lactobacillus fructivorans, tolerate acid and low pH well enough to live in it. *Inference —* a dip that breaks and a dip that spoils is a dip a bar has to make often or buy carefully, which is part of why the cup is a house signature in Buffalo and a pumped condiment elsewhere.

Steve Henson (1918–2007), a Thayer, Nebraska native, worked as a plumbing contractor in the Anchorage area and cooked for his own crews. He put together the dressing in the early 1950s. He retired from plumbing at 35, moved with his wife Gayle to Santa Barbara County, California, and in 1956 bought a guest ranch in San Marcos Pass that they renamed Hidden Valley Ranch.

Guests at the ranch steakhouse bought jars to take home. The first commercial customer was Henson's friend Audrey Ovington, who owned Cold Spring Tavern. By 1957 Henson was selling packets of dry mix in stores, and by mail at 75 cents apiece, eventually giving over every room in the house to the operation. The guest ranch closed by the mid-1960s; the mail-order business did not. Clorox bought the brand in October 1972 for $8 million and Henson retired. The name is why a federal court in Fort Worth spent 1976 deciding who else could write 'ranch style' on a label.

sections.h: How ranch got onto the wing
sections.text: Ranch spread as a flavour before it spread as a wing dip. Clorox added buttermilk flavouring so the mix could be made with ordinary milk, and in 1983 developed a shelf-stable bottle. Cool Ranch Doritos arrived in 1987 and Hidden Valley Ranch Wavy Lay's in 1994. In 1992 ranch passed Italian to become the best-selling salad dressing in the United States. In 1994 Domino's began offering ranch as a condiment with its chicken wings and its pizzas, and the pairing took. *Inference —* the wing did not choose ranch; the delivery pizza chain put a cup of it in the box, and the wing was in the same box.

sections.h: The numbers, and whose they are
sections.text:
The National Chicken Council — the trade association for the producers, which is worth knowing when reading its polling — has run the question through Harris Poll for years. In the survey fielded 9 to 11 January 2018 among 2,086 US adults, of whom 1,381 eat wings, the sides and sauces typically eaten with wings ranked: ranch 59%, buffalo or hot sauce 48%, barbecue sauce 48% (those two tied), honey mustard 35%, blue cheese 33%, teriyaki 23%, sriracha 15%. The council noted ranch had climbed steadily, from 51% in 2014 to 56% in 2015.

Separately, the Association for Dressings and Sauces found in 2017 that 40% of Americans named ranch their favourite dressing outright. Ranch has led the US salad dressing category since 1992.

*Inference —* none of these figures is a count of dips poured beside wings. They are answers to a survey question, and they are the closest public measure that exists.

Wingstop makes its ranch in the restaurant every day and has built marketing around it: in March 2026 it released a limited-edition 32-ounce cup of ranch, and its chief brand officer Donnie Upshaw said "Our fans turned our housemade ranch into a phenomenon, and when the love is this real, subtlety doesn't make sense." The chain makes its bleu cheese fresh in the morning too. It publishes no ratio between the two.

*Inference —* no chain I could find publishes how many cups of each it sells, which means the loudest evidence in this argument is marketing, not accounting.

sections.h: The argument, as each side puts it
sections.text: Buffalo's case is provenance and fit: blue cheese was on the plate first, its sharpness and its fat sit against cayenne and vinegar differently than a herbed buttermilk mayonnaise does, and the city's shops send it out unasked. Ranch's case is that most people asked say they prefer it, that it is milder and reads as less demanding of the eater, and that it is already in the box. Both positions are held sincerely and loudly, and neither is a claim this project settles.

No public series counts dip cups at a wing counter. Retail scanner data that would show ranch and blue cheese dollar sales side by side is sold by subscription, by Circana and by NielsenIQ, and is not open. Restaurant point-of-sale data is private to the chains. So the argument runs on survey answers, category share for bottled dressing sold in grocery stores, and what a bar hands you — three different things, none of them the same measurement.

text.what: A chicken wing has three joints and yields two pieces a kitchen will sell: the drumette, which is the humerus with the meat pushed to one end, and the flat, which is the two-boned middle section carrying most of the skin. The tip goes to stock. One bird gives one of each per wing, in a fixed ratio nobody can change, which is the whole economics of the argument: a counter can let you order all flats, but it cannot buy a bird that grows two of them. Federal regulation names the drumette and declines to name the flat. Survey respondents prefer the drum by a wide margin and split sharply by who is answering. No public price series prices one piece against the other.

sections.text:
Cut the wing at both joints and you have three pieces. Two get sold, one gets boiled. Every whole wing therefore yields exactly one drumette and exactly one flat. An order of twenty is twenty pieces, ten birds' worth of one wing each, and left alone it arrives ten and ten.

*Inference —* that fixed one-to-one is why 'all flats' is the only common wing request that costs the seller something real. Every other modification — sauce, heat, extra crisp, dip on the side — changes what leaves the kitchen. This one changes what is left in it.

Title 9 of the Code of Federal Regulations, section 381.170(b), defines the cuts. Item (7): "'Wings' shall include the entire wing with all muscle and skin tissue intact, except that the wingtip may be removed." Item (18): "'Wing drummette' consists of the humerus of a poultry wing with adhering skin and meat attached." Item (19): "'Wing portion' consists of a poultry wing except that the drummette has been removed."

The flat has no federal name. It is defined by subtraction — what is left of a wing once the drumette is gone — and spelled 'drummette' with two m's on the way there. *Inference —* the counter's vocabulary ran ahead of the regulator's, which is usual, and the regulator has not caught up.

Flat, drum, drumette, party wing, wingette, mid-joint. A grocery bag labelled party wings holds both pieces already split. A counter that asks 'flats or drums?' is offering something most places will not, and a menu line reading ALL FLATS +$ is telling you the same thing in money.

CivicScience put the question to 6,093 US consumers and published the result on 5 June 2014: 45% of wing-eaters prefer drums, 29% the flats, and 26% like both equally.

The splits are sharper than the topline. Men chose drums over flats 40% to 20%; women 29% to 24%. Black respondents went the other way, 43% for flats against 30% for drums. Hispanic respondents went hardest for drums, 47% to 16%. Self-described cooking enthusiasts were 32% more likely than average to choose flats; sports enthusiasts chose drums 40% to 17%.

That survey is twelve years old as of 2026 and I found no newer public one at the same sample size. Read it as the best available figure, not the current one.

Two thin bones, and between them a strip of meat under a wider sheet of skin than the drumette carries for its weight. Fry it and more of the piece is crackle; sauce it and more of the piece is sauced, because the surface-to-meat ratio is higher. It pulls apart: twist the bones out and the meat comes free in one piece. *Tradition holds —* the flat is the cook's cut, and the CivicScience finding that cooking enthusiasts skew toward it is consistent with that.

One bone, a handle at the narrow end, meat pushed into a lump at the other. It eats in two bites without engineering, it dips one-handed, and it holds heat longer because the mass is thicker. *Tradition holds —* the drum is what a plate of wings looks like in a photograph, which is not nothing when the wings are being sold.

USDA Agricultural Marketing Service, Weekly National Chicken Report, for 7 to 11 September 2026: Wings – Whole traded at a weighted average of 110.02 cents per pound, in a range of 82.00 to 136.00, on 507,000 pounds, down 2.35 cents from the previous week's 112.37. In the same table drumsticks ran 55.35 cents, boneless-skinless breast 121.35, and backs and necks stripped 10.91.

The series prices the wing whole. There is no line for a flat and no line for a drumette. USDA's retail report is the same: it carries 'Party Wings, Flats and Drums' as one item — 2,022 stores advertising conventional fresh at a weighted $3.27 per pound in the week of 5 to 17 September 2026 — and prices V-Cut Wings separately, but never a flat on its own.

So the premium a bar charges for all flats has no public benchmark behind it. I could not obtain a foodservice price list that separates the two cuts; the distributors that publish case prices refused this project's requests on 16 September 2026, and the subscription series that poultry traders use, Urner Barry's, is not open. That absence is itself the answer to 'what does a flat cost' — nobody publishes it.

sections.h: What a shop does with the drums
sections.text:
*Inference —* a counter that sells all-flats orders has three ways out, and they are all visible on menus. It can buy pre-separated flats from a processor, paying whatever that costs and leaving the drum problem upstream. It can charge an upcharge large enough that the drums it is left holding are already paid for. Or it can move the drums somewhere else on the menu — the mixed basket, the lunch special, the platter, the dry-rub tray — and price those to clear.

The same logic runs in reverse at a shop that sells mostly drums, which then has flats to move. Neither shop is doing anything unusual; it is the arithmetic of a bird with one of each.

The third segment goes by wing tip, flapper or pointer. It is mostly skin, cartilage and bone, and it is where a kitchen's stock comes from. Some shops leave it attached to the flat and sell the two-piece section as it comes off the bird, which changes the count on the plate and the price per pound in the buyer's favour or the seller's, depending how the menu is written.

text.what: Two Buffalo kitchens claim the wing, and neither claim rests on a document. The Anchor Bar dates the dish to the night of 4 March 1964 and tells the story three different ways. John Young was selling breaded whole wings in a tomato sauce he called mumbo from 1961, registered his shop's name at the county courthouse, and said the Anchor Bar carried no wings as a regular menu item until 1974. A 1969 newspaper profile of the Anchor Bar does not mention wings. Duff's started selling them across town that same year. The city proclaimed a Chicken Wing Day in 1977, Calvin Trillin carried the story out of western New York in 1980, and the National Buffalo Wing Festival put John Young in its Hall of Flame in 2013. This page lays out who claims what and on what evidence.

sections.text: Chicken wings were cheap in the early 1960s because almost nobody ordered them. A wing went into stock, into soup, or into the bin. Every version of the origin story starts from that fact and explains what changed it. *Inference —* the cheapness matters more than the invention: a dish made of a throwaway cut can appear in several kitchens at once without anybody copying anybody.

sections.h: The Anchor Bar, told three ways
sections.text:
Frank and Teressa Bellissimo opened the Anchor Bar on Main Street in 1935. Their son Dominic told the wing story for thirty years, and the family told it in at least three shapes.

In the first, Dominic was tending bar late one night, friends of his arrived unannounced, and Teressa wanted something fast to put in front of them, so she deep-fried wings and tossed them in cayenne hot sauce.

In the second, which Dominic gave Calvin Trillin in 1980, the clock did the work. Trillin reports him saying it was a Friday night, people were buying a lot of drinks, and he wanted to do something nice for them at midnight, when the mostly Catholic drinkers could eat meat again.

In the third, Frank told it as an accident of delivery: wings arrived instead of the backs and necks the bar cooked into its spaghetti sauce, and faced with them he asked Teressa to do something. In every version Teressa sends the wings out with celery and blue cheese, and the first plates go out free.

The house pins it to 4 March 1964 — Dominic behind the bar, friends arriving late, little food left, wings meant for soup going into the fryer with butter and cayenne. That date is the claim's spine. *Inference —* a date that specific, attached to a night no receipt survives from, is the part of the story a reader should hold most loosely; it is also the part the Anchor Bar has never moved.

John Young moved to Buffalo from Stockton, Alabama in 1948, aged thirteen. From 1961 he sold uncut chicken wings — breaded, deep-fried, and served in a tomato-based sauce he called mumbo — at John Young's Wings 'n Things. He said a travelling boxer had told him about a restaurant in Washington, D.C. doing good business in wings, and that he decided to specialise. He registered the shop's name at the county courthouse and left the Buffalo area in 1970.

In a later interview Young said the Anchor Bar did not offer Buffalo wings as a regular menu item until 1974. His wing is not the Anchor Bar's wing: it is whole, it is breaded, and the sauce is tomato rather than cayenne and butter. *Inference —* that difference cuts both ways. It weakens any claim that one shop copied the other, and it complicates the question the argument is usually asked in, which assumes one dish with one inventor.

sections.h: 1969, and what a newspaper left out
sections.text: A local newspaper wrote up the Anchor Bar in 1969 and did not mention wings. Duff's, across town, began selling them that year; Duff's itself dates to 1946 under founder Louise Duffney and only took the wing into its name in 1985. *Inference —* a profile that skips the dish is not proof the dish was absent, but it sits badly beside a claim that the bar had been selling it for five years.

sections.h: The city settles nothing, and celebrates
sections.text: In 1977 the city of Buffalo issued a proclamation honouring Frank Bellissimo and declared 29 July 1977 Chicken Wing Day. A proclamation is an act of civic affection, not a finding of fact; it names one man and one bar, and it is the oldest official document in the argument.

Calvin Trillin had written the New Yorker's U.S. Journal since 1967, reporting local events across the country. In 1980 he turned the column on the Buffalo wing and published An Attempt to Compile a Short History of the Buffalo Chicken Wing. The title is the argument in miniature: an attempt, a compilation, a short history. The piece carried the Anchor Bar's version out of western New York and into the national record, and it is where Dominic's midnight-Friday telling is preserved.

At the National Buffalo Wing Festival in 2013, John Young was inducted into the festival's National Buffalo Wing Hall of Flame — the festival's own recognition, given by the event Drew Cerza founded in 2002.

In November 2021 a mural went up at Jefferson and Carlton, the corner where Young's first Wings 'n Things stood. John Baker and the WNY Urban Arts Collective installed it, recreating an original work by William Cooper and Dalton Easton that had hung inside the shop. Buffalo Bike Tours raised more than $12,000 for it through a GoFundMe, wing pop-ups, and grants from the Baird Foundation and the Buffalo Niagara Medical Campus. Family members of Young stood at the unveiling.

No menu from 1964 names a wing. No receipt, no photograph, no order slip, no supplier invoice for the mistaken delivery has been produced by anyone in sixty years of arguing. The Anchor Bar's account reaches the record through the family telling it, and the earliest published telling anyone cites is Trillin's, sixteen years after the night in question — which is testimony, not paper. John Young's account reaches the record the same way, through an interview given long after 1961.

The one dated document either side names is the courthouse registration of John Young's Wings 'n Things, and it dates the name of a shop, not the dish sold in it. The 1969 newspaper profile is the only contemporaneous paper anybody cites, and it is evidence of an absence, which is the weakest kind there is.

*Inference —* the argument is unresolvable on the evidence that exists, and both sides know it. That is why it is conducted in proclamations, trademarks, halls of fame and murals: every one of those is a way of settling a question that the documents will not settle.

sections.h: How the claims are held now
sections.text: The Anchor Bar trademarked the phrase and runs 18 locations as of 2026, and its sauces sell through Tops and Wegmans in the United States and Sobey's and Metro in Canada. Duff's trades on the rivalry and has locations across western New York, Rochester, Texas and the Toronto area. Visit Buffalo runs a Buffalo Wing Trail that lists fourteen stops and puts the Anchor Bar and Duff's on the same list. Young's claim is held by a mural, a hall-of-fame induction, and the people who keep repeating it.

text.what: In 1964 the wing was the cheapest thing on the bird, which is the premise every origin story rests on. In the week of 7 to 11 September 2026 it traded wholesale at 110.02 cents a pound, twice the price of a drumstick and ten times the price of the backs and necks that the Anchor Bar story says were supposed to arrive instead. It has been dearer than that: 325 cents a pound in May 2021, when cold storage ran to its lowest level since 2012. Every figure on this page carries its date and whose figure it is, and the ones I could not get are named too.

sections.h: The cheap end of the bird
sections.text: Chicken wings were inexpensive and undesirable in the early 1960s, normally thrown away or kept back for stock or soup. That is the condition the Buffalo story turns on and the condition that has been reversed. *Inference —* the reversal is the dish's doing: a cut only becomes expensive once people order it by name.

Two USDA series carry most of the weight here, and both are free to read.

The Weekly National Chicken Report, from the Agricultural Marketing Service's Livestock, Poultry and Grain Market News, prices parts in cents per pound, domestic, fresh, conventional, FOB, with a weighted average, a range, the week's volume, and the previous week for comparison.

The Weekly Grocery Store Chicken Feature Activity report gives advertised retail prices in dollars per pound, with the number of sampled stores running each ad, drawn from store circulars, newspaper ads and retailer websites.

The National Chicken Council publishes a Chicken Wing Report each January, which is the number newspapers print. It is a trade association's estimate for a single Sunday.

sections.h: What a wing costs a buyer this week
sections.text:
Weekly National Chicken Report, 7 to 11 September 2026. Wings – Whole: range 82.00 to 136.00 cents a pound, weighted average 110.02, on 507,000 pounds, down 2.35 cents from the previous week's 112.37 on 517,000 pounds.

The rest of the bird, same table, same week, in cents per pound: boneless-skinless breast 121.35, boneless-skinless thighs 148.48, tenderloins 113.50, bone-in thighs 72.89, bone-in legs 71.12, drumsticks 55.35, leg quarters in bulk 52.76, backs and necks stripped 10.91, frames 9.66.

Read down that list against the Anchor Bar's third version of its own story — the one where backs and necks were ordered and wings turned up by mistake. In September 2026 the mistake would have cost roughly ten times what the order did.

USDA's Economic Research Service published the account on 11 March 2022, drawing on its February 2022 Livestock, Dairy, and Poultry Outlook.

Pandemic demand for takeout wings pulled cold storage down to its lowest level since 2012. Supply-chain disruption dropped inventories a further 27% by January 2021. In April 2021 wholesale wing prices ran 180% above a year earlier. They peaked at $3.25 a pound in May 2021. As cold storage recovered from May onward, prices fell through the rest of the year; by January 2022 wings were $2.68 a pound — 24 cents above January 2021, and 49 cents below the 2021 peak.

In February 2018 The Counter reported jumbo wings at $2.16 a pound wholesale while boneless breast meat traded at $1.03 — the wing at more than twice the price of the cut a boneless wing is made from. On Super Bowl Sunday 2015 wings had gone for $1.91.

In the week of 7 to 11 September 2026 the relationship has flipped back: boneless-skinless breast at 121.35 cents, wings at 110.02. *Inference —* a restaurant deciding this month whether to push bone-in or boneless faces a different arithmetic than one deciding it in 2018, and the menu category that got built during the inversion has outlived the price gap that built it.

Weekly Grocery Store Chicken Feature Activity, issued 11 September 2026, for ads running 5 to 17 September 2026. Prices are dollars per pound, weighted across the stores advertising the item.

Party Wings, Flats and Drums, conventional, fresh, regular pack: $3.27 across 2,022 stores, against $2.93 the previous week and $3.99 a year earlier. Value pack: $2.88 across 1,479 stores. Antibiotic-free regular: $4.67 across 406 stores. Frozen IQF, conventional: $3.28 across 4,614 stores. V-Cut Wings, conventional, regular: $2.66 across 334 stores.

From the hot case, priced per piece rather than per pound: fried or baked bone-in wings in bulk at $0.90 a piece across 1,980 stores. The boneless line shows only a year-ago figure, $0.56 a piece across 15 stores.

The National Chicken Council released its Chicken Wing Report for Super Bowl LX on 28 January 2026: Americans would eat 1.48 billion wings watching the game, about 10 million more than the year before. The release runs the usual comparisons — the wings would circle the planet nearly three times, and hauling them would take more than 3,400 fully loaded semi-trucks.

On price the release cites Wells Fargo's Super Bowl Food Report: retail fresh wings averaging $3.47 a pound on a four-week moving average, down 2.8% year on year. Tom Super, the council's spokesman, is quoted: "I think Bradley Cooper is wrong: Football is for food. Especially when it comes to the Super Bowl, where wings rule the roost."

The release does not publish the method behind the 1.48 billion. *Inference —* an estimate without its method is a headline, and it is reprinted every January as though it were a count.

A wholesale series that prices a flat apart from a drumette. USDA's report prices Wings – Whole only, and its retail report bundles flats and drums into one line; the foodservice distributors that publish case prices refused this project's requests on 16 September 2026, and Urner Barry's series, which poultry traders use for exactly this, is sold by subscription.

A bar's own posted price. Menus for the Buffalo shops sit behind ordering platforms that serve nothing to a plain request; Bar-Bill and Duff's both refused on 16 September 2026. So the counter prices above are a grocery hot case, not a bar, and they are labelled as such.

A long price series in one place. The USDA reports are weekly snapshots; assembling a run of years from them means collecting week by week, and the ERS chart that does assemble one stops in early 2022.
